maintopic: ORGANIZATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that Canada will be represented at the ministerial meeting in Paris, July 22 and 23, to consider the proposed organization for economic co-operation and development. The Canadian delegation will be led by the Minister of Finance and will also include Mr. S. S. Reisman of the Department of Finance, Mr. O. G. Stoner of the Department of External Affairs, Mr. R. Campbell Smith of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Jules Leger, Canadian ambassador to NATO and the O.E.E.C., and Mr. Peter Towe of the Canadian mission to NATO and the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
It will be recalled that following the special meetings on economic co-operation in Paris in January, a group of four experts prepared a report and recommendations on the establishment of a new organization for economic co-operation and development to replace the organization for European economic co-operation. Canada and the United States would be full members of the new organization, which would be shaped to meet the problems of the 1960's.
This week in Paris ministers of the 18
O.E.E.C. member countries and Canada and the United States, together with representatives from the European communities, will be asked to approve provisionally a draft convention along the lines of the report and recommendations of the group of four, and to agree generally on the activities of the new organization. While all decisions that are made at this meeting will be provisional, they will be taken as an indication of willingness to sign a convention subsequently

subject, of course, to parliamentary ratification by the parliaments and legislative bodies of all participating governments.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will have heard with interest and approval the Prime Minister's announcement. The conference to which he referred is one that will be dealing with subjects of very far-reaching importance, as important to this country as to any of the countries that will be represented there. Therefore I think it is a matter for satisfaction that such a strong Canadian delegation is going to this conference in Paris headed by the Minister of Finance. I know that the minister is a very energetic and hard-working person, but how he is going to manage to be in Paris at that conference and in Ottawa at the conference with the provinces on fiscal relations is a little beyond our understanding, but no doubt he will be able to manage it somehow or other.

Mr. Speaker, we think that such a meeting and the formation of such an organization is long overdue. We think Canada has been tardy in taking action that was necessary as a result of the setting up of the common market and the outer seven. In this day and age, action by the Canadian government should be directed at all times toward removing barriers against international trade and toward a reduction of tariffs. We have said that Canada should associate herself initially with the outer seven and eventually with the whole north Atlantic trading area. Although this is something like locking the stable door after the horses are out, we hope this organization will get the horses back into the stable.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a very urgent question I want to ask the Minister of Agriculture. speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: FRASER VALLEY, B.C.    COMPENSATION UNDER BRUCELLOSIS CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the department has not been aware up to this time of any complaints from the Fraser valley in connection with the valuation of cattle ordered destroyed as a result of the brucellosis eradication program. However, the valuation and slaughtering procedures will be examined in order to assure full application of the intent of the valuation authority under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
Under the provisions of this act the maximum valuation for grade cattle is $70, and $140 for purebred cattle. In addition to this valuation the owner receives the beef value of the animal. In valuing grade animals three factors are taken into consideration: (1) conformation; (2) age; (3) immediate or prospective usefulness. Each factor is considered separately and is considered to represent one third of the value.
In valuing purebred, registered cattle, four factors are considered:	(1) pedigree; (2)
conformation; (3) age; (4) immediate or prospective usefulness. In this case, each factor is considered to represent one quarter of the total value.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED USE OF GERMAN IMMIGRANTS AS STRIKE BREAKERS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED USE OF GERMAN IMMIGRANTS AS STRIKE BREAKERS
speechtext:
On July 7 the hon. member for Assiniboia asked me a question with reference to a statement that Germans who were brought to Canada to act as technical advisers to Associated Mining Construction Limited of Esterhazy, Saskatchewan, were being used by that company in a type of strike-breaking role. I inquired from my department and found that an investigation was already on the way at the request of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Ormiston).
The situation at the potash mine in Ester-hazy, where a number of Canadian workers are on strike, has been investigated jointly by immigration and national employment service officials. To obtain experienced personnel to assist them in sinking a shaft through the Blairmore sands, the company had previously brought forward 12 employees of the parent company in Germany. Three of these are heads of the firm and nine are key personnel, such as civil engineers. They are legally in Canada.
When the strike began the company was obliged to use the services of nine German personnel for maintenance work. Their work pertains to hoists, freeze plant, electrical equipment and the maintenance of freeze holes at the bottom of the shaft. The company states that if these freeze holes are not maintained, the ice wall in the Blairmore formation could be permanently damaged.
The investigation carried out indicates the German personnel are being engaged only in essential maintenance work to protect the shaft, which it is understood represents an

investment of $5.6 million out of an investment which will total $24.5 million.

speakerposition: stagedirection

subtopic: REFERENCE OF CUBAN COMPLAINT AGAINST U.S. TO ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact that the United Nations security council is now giving consideration to sending the Cuban government's complaint against the United States to the organization of American states for its consideration and disposal, does the minister not consider that the security council remains the proper forum for the settlement of any dispute in the hemisphere of more than local importance, and that this action on the part of the United Nations security council is a surrender of a portion of its authority under the United Nations charter?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE OF CUBAN COMPLAINT AGAINST U.S. TO ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES
speechtext: I just raise this question for the consideration of the house. I am not sure whether the question asked does not go beyond the administrative responsibility of the government. It relates to foreign affairs and Canada is a member of the United Nations, but that seems to be the closest link. However, I do not wish to bar the minister from answering if he wishes to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF CUBAN COMPLAINT AGAINST U.S. TO ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this issue is under consideration in the security council this week, and I think the hon. member is right in asking this question. Of course I have the answer ready; it may well be that I might look on it a little differently if I had not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REFERENCE OF CUBAN COMPLAINT AGAINST U.S. TO ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES
speechtext: It is not a trouble-making question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF CUBAN COMPLAINT AGAINST U.S. TO ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES
speechtext:
The answer to the question is no. Action by the security council to refer a dispute to a regional organization is, in fact, recommended by the charter. In article 33 of chapter 6, entitled "Pacific Settlement of Disputes", it is stated among other things that parties to any dispute shall, first of all, seek solution by resort to regional agencies or arrangements. Paragraph 2 of the same article specifically authorizes the security council to call upon the parties concerned to settle their disputes by such means.
It may be of interest to the house if I read the full text of article 33:
Paragraph 1. The parties to any dispute, the continuance of which is likely to endanger the maintenance of international peace and security, shall, first of all, seek a solution by negotiation,

Inquiries of the Ministry inquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement, resort to regional agencies or arrangements-
And that, of course, is the material provision in this particular case.
-or other peaceful means of their own choice.
Paragraph 2. The security council shall, when it deems necessary, call upon the parties to settle their disputes by such means.

speechtext:
I should like to make a confession with regard to a question asked me yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition He asked, as reported at page 6409 of Hansard:
Can the minister inform the house whether the government has received any request from Katanga for recognition as a separate state.
I replied:
Not directly, Mr. Speaker, although an effort is being made by the government of Katanga to get recognition from various countries.
I checked that point after the orders of the day yesterday, and actually we did get a commercial telegram last Friday which purported to come from Mr. Tshombe, who is the premier of Katanga province and who is reported to have established himself as head of state of an independent Katanga. The telegram requested Canada's recognition. No reply has been sent.
This problem is part of the complex and rapidly changing Congo situation, and it is being studied. The whole Congo situation is, of course, being studied in consultation with other interested authorities.

speechtext:
Before this motion is passed, Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to move an amendment dealing with the plight in which our old age pensioners find themselves today. I am sure there is no one in this house who has not received letters from old age pensioners describing the piteous plight in which many of them find themselves in this country today. The last action taken by this government in regard to this group of people was back in 1957, just a couple of months prior to the 1958 election. I should like to remind hon. members of some of the words that were uttered by members of the cabinet at that time, which created an impression across this country that it would be only a short time before further action would be taken on behalf of these old age pensioners.
I should like to quote from Hansard for November 4, 1957 at page 714. I am quoting now the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith). He said: My hon. friend made reference to adjustments necessitated by the rising costs of living. The present adjustment in the old age benefit level is itself an adjustment to meet the rising cost of living. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind that if the cost of living continues to spiral in the future as it has in the past further adjustments will be necessary. This has been the experience with benefit levels ever since 1927. That is precisely why I said in my opening statement that we did not consider that there was anything final or sacred about the amount of $55 that is now proposed.
Old Age Pensions
There is another point, Mr. Speaker, which while not mentioned in the minister's words at that time, I believe has been accepted by almost everyone across this country, that is everyone who is in the plight of our old age pensioners today and who is dependent on the actions of the federal government, have a right to have considered when their plight is being discussed. I refer to the relationship of their pension to the gross national product. On more than one occasion, the Minister of Finance has pointed proudly to the fact that the gross national product has been increasing year by year, in some years more than in others.
In so far as the gross national product is concerned, many of the other groups, if you want to call them that, in our society have the ability and opportunity to take advantage of this general increase in productivity. Industry, for instance, is able to raise its prices so it can obtain a share of this increased national wealth. Labour, through the trade unions, is able to take economic action to ensure that, to some extent at least, labour gets its share of this increased wealth from year to year. However, the old age pensioners who, as I said before, are completely dependent on the action or lack of action of our federal government, have no means by which they can bargain or obtain their proper share of this increase in wealth in our country. I believe that everyone who has taken part in arbitration or conciliation boards, or who has considered the equitable distribution of wealth amongst the people in our society, has agreed that the increase in the wealth of our country should not apply to only certain groups in our society but should be considered in all groups in our society.
As the minister said some three years ago, it was the intention of the government at that time that should the cost of living continue to increase, the government would take some action in that regard. I should like to place a few figures on the record which are taken from the price index for May, 1960. I shall not deal with all the figures, but I should like to deal with the ones which most seriously affect the plight of our old age pensioners. We find that the total index in that period of time, from 1957 to May, 1960, has inceased from 121.9 to 127.4, an increase of 5.5 per cent. We find that shelter, which is something every one of our old age pensioners has to find for himself or herself through some means or other, has increased by 8.6 per cent, from 134.9 to 143.5. Clothing is an item which may not affect the old age pensioner to the same extent as some of the younger people, but this item has increased by 2.3 per cent, from 108.5 to 110.8.

Old Age Pensions
The next item is household operation, which includes fuel, furnishings, domestic gas, electricity and so on. We find this item has increased by 3.5 per cent, from 119.6 to 123.1. We go, then, to other commodities and services, which includes transportation, recreation, health care, drugs and so on. This item has increased by 11.5 per cent in that period, from 126.1 to 137.6. These increases point up the increasingly difficult situation in which our old age pensioners find themselves within this space of time since 1957, when their plight was last given some consideration.
There are only two more figures that I should like to place on the record, Mr. Speaker. They have to do with two of the cheapest cuts of meat to be found in the stores across the country. I am referring to stewing beef and hamburg. We find that from 1957 to May, 1960 stewing beef increased by 264 per cent, from 52.6 to 138.8, and that hamburg has increased by 327 per cent, from 37.9 to 124.
These few figures point out clearly that the situation of our old age pensioners, as has been shown by many letters that I have received-and I am sure other hon. members have received such letters-has deteriorated rapidly over the past three years. It is also clear that unless action is taken this situation will continue, and that unless some prodding is done by opposition members action will not be taken. At least to date, and this session is six months old, it does not appear that the government is wanting to take any action in this regard.
I would hope that at least once in this country we might have a government which would give some consideration to problems like these when a federal election was not in the offing. I would hope that this is one of the practices of the previous government that this government would discontinue. Unfortunately, however, that does not appear to be the case. The only action they took in this regard was just prior to their second election in 1958. There may be some people in the country who have no faith at all in this government.
Hear, hear.

I do not know that I would go quite that far because, just in these three years that we have been here, owing to the prodding and suggestions of the opposition, the government have finally come around to taking some action in certain fields. I might say that is one respect at least in which I disagree with my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur. While it might take some time, at least the suggestions and prodding of the opposition do have an effect on the government.

In order to back up this statement I should like to refer again to the same page of Hansard of November 4, 1957, in the second column, where we find that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is reported as follows:
I have noted also, Mr. Speaker, a number of suggestions from different quarters of the house, chiefly from C.C.F. and Social Credit members, that we should abolish altogether the restrictions on the length of temporary absences from Canada. The member for Fraser Valley wants us to pay an old age security benefit to pensioners in any country of the world. In this way, he says, our senior citizens will become ambassadors of good will for Canada. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) demanded that I have the decency to tell the house why we did not intend to abolish the provision limiting the length of absences from Canada.
We find that in these three years this suggestion has finally sunk into the mind of this government, so that during this session which is now drawing to a close they have taken this action which was suggested so strongly by members of this group some three years ago. It is my hope that they will take similar action with regard to this problem. With that thought in mind, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I move:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide for an increase in the old age pension to $75 per month.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I place this amendment before the house, has any hon. member any point to make? If not, is the house ready for the question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons why I think consideration must be given to this suggestion is the change in attitude in Canada toward this matter of maintaining the elderly citizens of our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Timiskaming will permit me to interrupt him, may I say that I was perhaps a little bit slow in accepting your invitation, Mr. Speaker, to comment on the motion. I draw your attention to the fact that this amendment- which incidentally is introduced at a time when we understood there had been some understanding, at any rate, that the house would go into committee of supply today without debate-has been put in the form that in the opinion of the house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide for an increase in the old age pension.
I draw your attention to the fact that the estimates of the Department of National

Health and Welfare have already been before the house. They contemplate the continuance of a rate of $55 per month for the old age pension. The estimates were reported by the committee and the resolution to adopt the report was passed in this house some days ago. The house having taken that action, Mr. Speaker, at the present session, I therefore submit that this motion cannot now be introduced and that it is out of order.

I should like, if I may, to say a word on the point raised by the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance seems to be under the erroneous impression that the old age pensions are determined by the passing of the estimates of the department. I should perhaps remind the minister that the old age pensions are a statutory charge as the result of a statute, and have nothing whatever to do with the passing of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare or of any other department. May I also say that the suggestion that a statute adopted in another session should, in the opinion of the house, be given consideration by the government is exactly in line with the traditions of the house.

I will not endeavour to add anything to the point that has been made by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. I think it is obviously an accurate one. I was about to make it myself, so there is no need to repeat it.
I want to say that as far as I am concerned and as far as we in this group are concerned, there was no understanding about unanimous consent on this particular motion. There was consultation as to what we would do with regard to the sixth supply motion, and we said that we would not wish to move any amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I understand the point made by the Minister of Finance, it is that the decision of the committee to pass the vote to provide the money for payment of the old age pensions pursuant to the statute in that regard, plus the adoption of that resolution, constitutes a decision on this matter by the house which would make it improper for the house to decide the same matter again. I rather think I accept the contrary view that was expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, namely that the vote is really not a decision on this matter.
If I may be permitted to do so, I should like to give a little further thought to the issue which has been raised, inasmuch as
Old Age Pensions
it is an important one. I will allow the debate to proceed on that basis, and will ask the hon. member for Timiskaming to continue.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was pointing out that the attitude in Canada has changed over the years with regard to the support we give to the elderly citizens of our country. Fifty years ago or one hundred years ago it was generally conceded in this country that the children of parents were responsible for the maintenance of those parents, just as the parents themselves had been responsible for the maintenance of the children in their formative years.
Over the years, Mr. Speaker, our attitude has changed. We are no longer capable of looking after our parents, particularly young people who get married and raise families of their own. They are not raising them on the homestead or on the farm or in a place where they can easily take care of their parents; they are raising them far removed from where their parents lived their lifetimes and in many cases far removed from the occupations their parents had followed. Therefore there has been a change in the method of supporting the older citizens of this country and a major change in the attitude toward children supporting their parents.
This has been a gradual change. There is no question but that some of the citizens of this country today are looking after their parents in exactly the same manner as their grandparents and their great grandparents were taken care of, but many of our citizens are being taken care of only through general contributions made by the Canadian people as a whole.
While the old age pension has been increased over the years, it has not been increased with any formula in mind and in many cases has not borne much relationship to the need of the old age pensioners. I think it could legitimately be argued that when the old age pension was first introduced in Canada the $20 paid at that time was probably greater in its purchasing ability than the $55 we now pay our senior citizens. In this respect I think we should congratulate the government, and stress on behalf of many of the old age pensioners the appreciation they have of the changes which have been made in the old age pension act.
The hon. member for Timmins pointed out a few moments ago that in referring to the matter of old age pensions a year ago the minister said that many of the changes we recommended could not take place. Yet in the short period of one year we have seen the old age pensioner put into a much better

Old Age Pensions
position in some respects than he was a year ago. I refer of course to the amendments passed this year which allow the old age pensioners to live in other countries than Canada on pretty nearly a permanent basis.
In changing our attitude toward the maintenance of our elderly citizens, I believe we must also take into consideration how we will finance them. At the present time we say in this amendment that the amount which the old age pensioners receive should be $75, and I suggest that this is only a basic pension and will not be sufficient to keep a person in some of the cities in Canada today. I would also think that $75 paid to an old age pensioner who has his own home and lives on a little piece of land may be quite sufficient to maintain him in a very reasonable and respectable manner.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we come to the problem of how we are to finance this change. When the contributions were set up the old age pension was $40 a month. Since that time we have increased it twice but have made no change or very little change in the method of financing it. It seems to me that we should give some consideration now, not in four or five years' time, to some of the suggestions made in the Clark report, to some of the conclusions they came to and the comparisons they made between plans in the United States and Great Britain and some of the European countries and plans in Canada at the present time.
I also think we should take into consideration some of the arguments for a contributory plan in Canada or a plan which in the main comes from general revenues, with the advantages of both types of plans, and then come to a conclusion as to which plan will suit the immediate needs of the Canadian people in order to establish a decent and respectable pension for our senior citizens. I think the trend which has developed under which we collectively look after them on an individual basis makes it imperative for all Canadians to give to the old age pensioners and the senior citizens of this country an opportunity to gain the most out of the years of their retirement and to take the best advantage of the money we make available for this purpose. At the same time this will allow them to make as great a contribution toward that retirement as they can during the years they have to support this type of program.
Mr. Speaker, if we wait until the day when it is absolutely necessary to pay our citizens $100 or $150 a month for maintenance, it will be too late to change the method of contributions to allow you or me to contribute toward a retirement fund, and we

will be asking our children to contribute to something we should have changed in order to allow us to establish a better retirement pension.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that is what the old age pension is now becoming; it is becoming a retirement fund on a national basis. I think in recommending that the pension be raised to $75 we are only establishing the minimum which will apply now, but which will not be applicable in another year or in a very short period of time after. I believe in making this recommendation it is absolutely necessary to give consideration to the method by which we raise the money. It is true that we took the ceiling off the $60 and raised it to $90, but this is still a very unrealistic figure. In my opinion that ceiling should be removed entirely, because this is one of the methods we will have to use in order to raise the pension to $75 if we are going to continue the same type of scheme.
However, at the same time I think it is absolutely necessary for us to give close consideration to the whole matter of retirement funds, including our present national pension plan. This of course should take into consideration the plans now being supported by the Canadian people, whether they are of the insurance investment type or plans operated on a joint basis by collective agreements between labour and management, superannuation plans and all the other plans which go to make up our national retirement schemes.
In my opinion we are moving in the right direction; where our senior citizens ought not to depend on their children for their bread and butter in their retirement years; where we have set up a scheme under which they will be self-reliant and able to continue making a contribution to Canada. I am not one of those people who believe you can say that a person is too old to be of any value at 40, 50, 60, 70 or even 90 years of age. Some people at 90 years of age make a great contribution to the welfare of the country, and I do not think we can set an age limit to it. It is distressing to hear that people as young as 35 seeking jobs in industry are refused employment because of existing pension plan arrangements, which are based on the age of the company's employees and render the contributions too high. The entire Canadian retirement program should be brought under one roof, as it were. There is no better place to bring it than under the roof of the federal government. This will not necessarily eliminate all other plans, but will serve to eliminate those that are poor and unsuitable and those with no vesting rights.

We should pay our old age pensioners a reasonable amount based on the cost of living and the standard of living to which we are accustomed. It is not sufficient to provide old age pensioners with a roof over their heads and a subsistence diet consisting of bread, milk, butter and a small amount of meat. In arriving at a figure we should take into consideration the gross national product and the ability of Canadians to contribute to a plan that will enable our senior citizens to retire on decent standards. The time has come to consider this.
In my dealings with employees in various industries throughout the years I have never encountered any reluctance on their part to contribute to retirement funds, whether it be the old age pension scheme or a pension plan between the employee and employer. In every case, however, I found a great resentment on the part of the employee concerning those conditions that made it necessary for him to remain in the same job in the same plant under the same employer for a period of 25 years or more before receiving any benefit from the pension plan. These plans should be national in scope. People who retire should be granted a basic pension of $75 a month, and it would be advantageous for the Canadian economy and in the best interests of the security of our people if they could have a supplementary retirement pension equal to half the maximum salary they earned during their lifetime. Where the government contributed to the pension plan the $75 would be part of the retirement fund.
There is not an old age pensioner in the country who is not grateful to the Conservative government, and particularly to the Prime Minister, because an increase in the old age pension was granted at a time when pensioners themselves and Canadians in general felt that the pensioners had been slighted by the payment of a $6 increase under the Liberal administration. Because the Conservative government granted an increase to $55 and introduced useful provisions affecting pensioners resident outside the country, old age pensioners are still in sympathy with the government. The government therefore has a responsibility toward them to further increase the pension in keeping with present needs.
I do not ask the government to adopt $75 as a fixed figure. It could be increased to this amount today, but within a month or six months if the Canadian dollar continued to decline it might be that $75 would be too much and the economy could not bear it. On the other hand the rising cost of food, rent, clothing and medical care has made it imperative that the old age pensioner now receive $75. The government should examine 79951-0-410
Old Age Pensions
more closely than it has the recommendations of the Clark report and conduct an investigation of the feasibility of their implementation. The problem of old age pensioners could be solved in a way that would not cost the country too much money.
I sympathize with the argument that we cannot increase the pension under the present system of collecting moneys. If that is true the government should examine other methods of financing a program of this kind. A reasonable old age pension should be introduced in addition to a national portable contributory pension plan that would enable employees to retire with a pension equal to at least half their maximum salary earned during their working lifetime regardless of what industry or field they were engaged in.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution gives us an opportunity of discussing a matter which this parliament must consider from time to time as one of its first and most important duties in the field of social welfare. An examination of our senior citizens reveals that year by year they will increase in numbers. The number of people in Canada who will reach age 65 in 1970 will present a very considerable problem to governments on both the federal and provincial levels. We welcome the opportunity to remind the government of its responsibilities in connection with assistance to our senior citizens.
Some of the remarks made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat were not too easy to follow in view of the definite character of the amendment before the house, wherein it is proposed that there shall be an increase in the old age pension to $75 per month.
The hon. member, unwittingly or not, suggested that this amount might be lower, depending upon the circumstances. He did not have the same definiteness in his statement that one certainly found in the observations made by the proposer. It seems to me that the resolution must be approached from two points of view; (a) on its merits and (b) in so far as the responsibility of the government is concerned. It raises issues which we have to face.
The government certainly has a responsibility in this matter in the light of the assurances which it gave to the Canadian people. I hold in my hand a statement of the national leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Canada, issued in 1957.

Let us see the picture.

Old Age Pensions

Someone says "Let us see the picture". There is the picture. I quote:
It's time for a Diefenbaker government. A new national policy.
At the end of this pamphlet is the signature of the leader. Here is what the leader said and repeated in 1957:
Human betterment is of the essence of government and we intend to maintain all social security measures; we intend to maintain a high standard of social security to keep pace with the rising productivity of the nation.
That is the argument put forward by the hon. member for Timmins. The gross national product has increased. That being so, our pensions to our senior citizens should be increased, pursuant to the assurance given the Canadian people by the Prime Minister of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were.

My hon. friend says they were. They were two years ago, but we are now dealing with the situation which arises as a result of the small increase in the gross national product. My friend says they were; while it is true they were, let me remind him that the taxation policies of my hon. friend took back over 75 per cent of whatever increase was provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is untrue; it is so silly.
It is not untrue; it is a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is silly.

As a result of the tax policies of my hon. friend, who now interrupts, whatever increases were provided in the basic old age pension were taken away by policies of the very government that takes credit for the increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that is an untrue statement, utterly untrue.

My hon. friend always embellishes his interruptions so substantially with those generalizations which more and more put him in the position where we are not to regard his interruptions or take them seriously.
Nor yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
When I am finished, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very appropriate at this moment.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was the hon. member not a member of a government which in 1957 said that an increase from $40 to $46 a month in the old age pension was quite adequate?
Let me tell my hon. friend that I was a member of a government that provided $46 of the present pension; I was a member of a government-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not fair.

-that put on the
statute books of our country every single act of social legislation which is now in existence. I was a member of a government that provided the basis of all of the amendments brought in by this government in the field of social welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member answer my question about the $46 a month?

I was not a member of a government supporting this statement, again signed by the leader of the Conservative party, who said:
The Conservative party proposes to set the amount at a figure high enough to meet the needs of our older citizens and these other deserving persons, and to make necessary adjustments thereafter on a cost of living basis.
I was not a member of a government that made that kind of promise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You stopped at $46.

The minister
always finds himself embarrassed, and he continually interrupts in that usual, dignified manner, so characteristic of ministers of finance in this country. He and his colleagues did pledge to the Canadian people that they would increase old age pensions in accordance with the increase in the cost of living-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We did increase old age pensions.
-and with the rising productivity of the nation. My hon. friend was also a member of a government-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about $46?

-that said this:
A Progressive Conservative government will consider expanding the present old age pension system by the addition of an insurance system similar to that in the United States. The United States plan of old age and survivor insurance provides average monthly benefits on retirement of $76 for single workers, $128 for aged married couples without dependants, and $65 for aged widows.
The Prime Minister said in this signed statement:
The average contribution per person is $27.08 not much more than the average contribution by Canadians of $22.70 for the old age pension.

Listen to this:
A Conservative government will consider implementing such a plan-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did.

-"in addition to" the present pensions system.
My hon. friend says it did. My hon. friend, of course, does not know what he is talking about.
You do not know yourself.

The Prime Minister continued:
The United States plan is "worthy of the highest commendation."
The Minister of Finance says that this government has adopted this United States plan in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not; nothing of the kind.
You were not listening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member explodes let me say to him-
I have the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order,-
You may make your speech later; there is no point of order here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have at least to listen to the minister to see whether there is a point of order; 1 cannot decide it in advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is attributing to me a statement that I did not make. He has just been asking a series of rhetorical questions. I tried to ask him a question which he did not wish to answer, and I made a statement in regard to this series of rhetorical questions as to what this government had done in the light of promises made. That is what I commented on, and he is seeking now to distort my comments.

As we both anticipated, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend had no real point of order in mind.
With regard to this United States proposal, it would resolve the problem if the government would carry out its promise to implement the United States old age survivor system. Then this particular amendment would not be necessary, because, as the Prime Minister said in the promises which he made to the Canadian people, amounts of over $75 a month would be paid, depending upon the 79951-0-4101
Old Age Pensions
rate of contribution to that scheme, a scheme that is fully contributory. What is the situation? Not only has the government failed to implement its promises-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have implemented our promises; we raised the pension.

I am talking about the United States system. When my hon. friend says that he is ignoring the terrible contempt which this government has for the Canadian people and for the Canadian parliament in the repeated replies given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare with regard to the Clark report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about the $46 a month?

In 1958 the Prime Minister of this country stood in this house and said that he wanted to implement the United States system. This was shortly before the election of that year, and to that end he was going to appoint Professor Huson to make a report on the United States system. That report had to be completed in four months, which coincided, as a matter of fact, with the election date, in order that the government could implement this United States old age security system.
What is the situation? Professor Huson said he could not make a report in four months. Professor Clark was appointed in his place. The election took place, and there was no concern on the part of the Prime Minister or on the part of the ubiquitous Minister of Finance to see that this report was prepared in four months. Only two weeks ago, after almost two years of study, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that this report continues to receive study by the government.
If the government want to implement their promises, let the government act on the Clark report. Let them act in accordance with what the Prime Minister said, that the United States plan is worthy of the highest commendation, and in that way they will be able in part to meet the particular proposal involved in this amendment. Does the government now intend to implement the Clark report? I ask the Minister of Finance, who will have the final say in this matter as the watchdog of the treasury, does he stand in the way of the desire of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to see that we have the Clark report implemented in Canada? Is the Minister of Finance, who seeks to extricate himself from his present embarrassment by the synthetic smile he now has on his face-

Old Age Pensions

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a smile, it is a laugh. I am laughing at you; I cannot help it.
Does he propose to continue to stand in the way of the realization of this plan? Is he in favour of this plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What a sham.
Is the government in favour of the plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What a sham you are putting on here.
My hon. friend says, "What a sham".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I say to my hon. friend, who continually, and rightly so, is proud of his integrity in public life, does he think it is proper for a political party to make the kind of promises that I have read, promises that were made to the Canadian people-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And carried out.
-and then two years later look upon them in a lighthearted manner and say that they are continuing to study this report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those promises were carried out to the letter.
My hon. friend continues to say that the United States plan has been adopted by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it has been carefully studied. That is the point.

That is not what the Prime Minister said. He said that the United States plan was worthy of the highest commendation. He said that after four months' study we would see to the adoption of that plan. What is the position of our party on this subject? We stated our position in 1958 at a national convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Forty six dollars a month.

That position is immediate consideration of a national contributory pension scheme co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security pensions, to begin at 65 and to be based upon federal government contributions as well as upon contributions of employees, employers and self-employed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why, if he advc [DOT] cates that policy today-
I said that is our party's position now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, first of all perhaps the hon. member would indicate whether he subscribes to his party's position. If so, would he tell us why, in view of his boasts about his record when he was minister of national health and welfare, he did not inaugurate such a policy in all the years when he was minister of that department?

That is a fair question. I will say this to the minister, that he will not be able to find any assurance that I gave or that Mr. St. Laurent gave or that any members of that administration gave that was not fully implemented.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then you did not
advocate such a policy in those days?
The record is an impressive one-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Forty six dollars a month.

-family allowances, unemployment insurance, disability pensions, the veterans' charter, old age assistance, national hospital insurance. Most of these measures, in one form or another, were opposed by the party-
Don't forget the bubble gum tax.
-that now seeks to establish itself as the champion of social welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is untrue.

We have not had one expression of view from the government about its position in the matter of portable pensions, one of the live topics now in the field of social welfare. We do not know where the government stands. The position of this party and the position of the party immediately to our right have been expressed, but this government has given no indication where it stands on this matter. Are we to go on day after day, two years after the election, with the Clark report gathering dust on the desk of the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Is it going to lie there forever, or is the government going to wait until the eve of an election?
That is what you did.
The hon. member says that is what we did. If he will examine the record he will see that everything we did in the field of old age security was done

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 3 p.m.

Speaking on the particular subject to which this amendment directs our attention, I am sure I am warranted in referring to the fact that we have just come from Laurier House, where the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), as well as members of both houses of parliament, attended a ceremony at which the Prime Minister unveiled a commemorative plaque. I could not help but think when we attended the ceremony how appropriate the present discussion is. In my judgment the matters that are before us now received their foundation in no more effective manner than by the contributions made by the former leader of the
Old Age Pensions
Liberal party, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, who said on July 25, 1944:
I have fought for measures of social security and national well-being in season and out of season, in parliament and out of parliament, in this country and in other countries. I have fought for them wherever the opportunity presented itself, and win or lose in the future, I intend to fight for them to the end of my days.
We in this party, having contributed, as I believe we have, in the way I indicated before the recess, to the development of a responsible system of social welfare in Canada, therefore are vitally concerned that, whatever treatment we are able to accord to our senior citizens should be on the basis of need and our capacity to meet that need. We have stated our position, in the light of new and developing situations, in our platform, as enunciated at the national Liberal convention which selected the Leader of the Opposition as the leader of the Liberal party. We affirmed the extension of old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age. We suggested the introduction of new pension plans with provision for the early vesting of benefits, so that if an employee changed his employment he would retain the advantages of pension contributions previously made by him and by his employer, so that in effect the pension would follow the man.
As I mentioned this morning in commenting on the position of the government in relation to the Clark report, we went on record as saying we were in favour of the consideration of a national contributory pension scheme, co-ordinated with the existing provisions for retirement and old age security, the pension to begin at age 65 and to be based upon federal government contributions as well as upon contributions by employees, employers and selfemployed.
In the last enunciation of our objectives we have varied from the United States survivor's scheme, because that scheme is based entirely, both in so far as administrative costs and benefits are concerned, on premiums paid by employers and employees. It seems to us that the realization of the recommendation in the amendment could be met, not entirely but could be met, by the implementation of that scheme based upon the consideration given to it by the Clark report.
We recognize that this is an important matter, but in the light of the assurances given by the government it is difficult to understand how such a report, now over two years old, should not have encouraged the responsible minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to say something more than that he was studying the report. There is a limit to one's capacity to study. There certainly must be a limit to the time a government can be

Old Age Pensions
allowed to study a problem, particularly in the light of the assurances given us in 1958.
There are other considerations that should be borne in mind in discussing this matter, one of which relates to certain classes of our senior citizens who are not covered by the universal system. There is a co-operative arrangement between the two senior levels of government, under which some of these senior citizens are provided for by basic grants by the federal and provincial governments, that is for those 65 and over. In some provinces supplementary payments are made, and in some provinces the supplemental allowances are greater than in other provinces.
I regret that the Minister of Finance, to whom my earlier remarks were more pointedly directed, is not in his seat at the moment, undoubtedly because he is preoccupied with government business elsewhere. I am going to suggest to him that when he meets the provinces on July 25 he will have an opportunity of learning from them what further they may be disposed to do, and of telling them what further may be done by the federal government to meet the need that does exist among so many of our senior citizens.
Of course the Minister of Finance will be interested in meeting the premier of Quebec, who has announced the intention of his government to provide supplementary allowances, I believe for the first time in that province. There will be an opportunity presented to the other provinces, no doubt, to indicate their willingness to meet the problems that confront our senior citizens.
This whole problem must, of course, be viewed in the light of what has been done to date. We are now spending more on health and welfare measures on federal account, I believe, than in any other department of government, more even than for national defence. I am not ashamed to think I was a member of the government that was responsible for programs involving by far the largest portion of this annual fixed expenditure, designed to provide in our free, highly industrialized society through family allowances, disability pensions, old age assistance, old age security, blindness allowance, the veterans' charter, unemployment insurance or hospital insurance, assistance to individuals who require such assistance.
I have said that I believe the job of trying to develop an over-all system of social security is not done. Indeed, perhaps it will never be done. It must be faced in the light of new situations. I say now to the government that in spite of the fact that we have

the universal old age pension system based as it is on the non-means test principle, there are many individuals in our country- and I am not saying that this is a new fact- many elderly people, who still need additional assistance.
I am sure that a careful analysis and examination of this problem, particularly with the provinces, will reveal that in the case of our senior citizens one of the most effective ways of giving that assistance, particularly in necessitous cases, is with regard to medical care. That is a subject that is now receiving vigorous current discussion in the United States. The problem is as current and as applicable there as it is here. There are many thousands of our senior citizens who need medical care assistance, which in so many thousands of instances they cannot provide by themselves.
It will be no answer to what I am saying to suggest that these problems have always existed, and that the situation I have outlined today is one that was existing at least in part at the time the government of which I was a member was in power. That, of course, is the argument that is often made. I simply reiterate that we in this party have no reason to be ashamed of what we did in that field. I repeat that every single act on our statute books in the matter of social welfare was placed there either under Mackenzie King or under Louis St. Laurent. That is the fact.
I have not denied that this government has brought in amendments to these basic acts which have provided additional assistance. That, of course, is true. Any government in office, surely, in the face of existing situations would meet problems that face it in this particular area from time to time. But it is not the fact, and it is inaccurate to suggest that the concept of social security we now have in this country arises out of policies originally initiated by hon. gentlemen opposite. That is not historically a fact, and there is no one in this house who will deny what I have said.
The problem now is what to do immediately. That is one of the projections of this amendment. I have suggested that one of the ways to meet this problem in part would be for the government now, two years after the event and one and a half years after the report has been placed in the hands of the responsible minister, to tell us whether or not the government now believes that the United States survivor system is one that should be made applicable to us in Canada. If it is applicable, then why should there be any hesitation on the part of the government in saying so? If it cannot be implemented forthwith, it cannot be because of

any pecuniary obligation that would be imposed on the government of the day, because that system does not call for payment in any particular from the government at all. The payments under that system are provided in their entirety by the contributors and the beneficiaries, the employers and the employees. Hence there would be no additional charge on the exchequer.
There may be other reasons why the government does not wish to bring the program forward. Those reasons ought to be stated to us because, a report having been received such a long time ago, I believe a government stands close to being in contempt of parliament when it does not reveal its intentions under the circumstances attending this particular report.
I also think the government, when it comes to consider what it is going to do when it meets with the provinces, might consider whether it is not prepared now to embark upon certain particular procedures in cooperation with the provinces in order to provide for necessitous cases that exist under our old age security system, the universal plan and our old age assistance program. This was pointed out by Mr. Cecile, the minister of welfare in the province of Ontario. It was pointed out vigorously by Mr. Bland, the deputy minister, who said only two months ago that they were not satisfied with the administration of the social welfare policies of the federal government. They had reference particularly to this matter of old age assistance and old age security. They both stand as proponents of the American plan.
I think we are entitled to know now if the government has gone back on its earlier conception, whether it disagrees with the position taken by the province of Ontario, or what steps it is prepared to take to meet at least these necessitous cases.
We will be told, of course, that this government increased the old age security payments from $46 to $55 a month. There is no doubt about that fact. But I would also point out that of that $55, $46 had been contributed by policies, on behalf of the Canadian taxpayers, conceived by Liberal governments, and that most of the advantage of the additional $9 was withdrawn by the additional taxation imposed on the people of Canada by the Minister of Finance in the three budgets he has introduced in this house.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this amendment affords us the opportunity of eliciting from the government its views as to what it is prepared to do in the field of assisting the
Old Age Pensions
aged of our country, in providing for portable pensions, and to implement a report which it said had to be prepared within four months, so important and so demanding was the situation at that time.
That was in 1953. The situation has not changed. The gross national product has increased slightly. There has been an increase in the cost of living. We were assured that when there was an increase in the cost of living and when there was an increase in the gross national product, there would be corresponding increases in the rate of pension benefits. Those were not assurances given by us. Those were assurances given by those who now sit on the treasury benches. Under our system of government there can be no other course open than for the government to reply to these allegations and to our request for a clear enunciation of policy, something that is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part this morning in the discussion on the amendment moved by the C.C.F. group in this house, I have no wish to pose as an expert in this matter; however, I would like to express my views with regard to the matter of old age pensions.
It is a matter which has given rise to discussions in various circles, in the past few years and to a wide variety of opinions.
I have here before me the expression of some views which I shall try to summarize so as not to waste the time of the house, as we consider the matter more fully.
As pointed out by the previous speakers, the report of the Clark commission was tabled in this house and has been referred to on various occasions. Previously, and since the beginning of this session, several questions have been asked on this subject. They are to be found in the English edition of Hansard on pages 166, 1793, 3725-26, 4059-60, 4558-59.
Mr. Speaker, before summing up the various opinions I have before me, I would like to quote a few words referring to Catholicism and social justice from the magazine Relations of February 1959. Among others the article contains the following words:
Those truths were recalled by Pius XII on March 11, 1951, in his address to the Spanish workers:
Without the church, the social question is insoluble; but the church alone cannot solve it. She needs the co-operation of the intellectual, economic and technical forces of public powers. As far as the church is concerned, vast and well considered programs have been submitted as a religious and moral basis for every social order . .. When the labour movement is assigned aims which the church cannot approve they are merely illusory

Old Age Pensions
values to which truth, human dignity, social justice and even the true welfare of all citizens are sacrificed.
And the magazine Relations adds:
Those words adequately sum up the relation of Catholicism with social justice. Though the achievement of social justice is not, strictly speaking, a function of Catholicism, the Catholic church cannot ignore this function because, up to a point, social justice conditions the very success of its spiritual mission. On the other hand, social justice alone can only achieve partial and invariably disappointing results. In that field, as in all truly human activity, it remains the ferment which leavens the dough. Catholicism alone directs human effort towards those real values on which the safeguard and the promotion of truth, human dignity and social justice ultimately depends.
Well, this security legislation with regard to our senior citizens, certainly provides social security and should be unreservedly approved.
Now, as I explained a moment ago, varying opinions were expressed on the matter, ranging from an extreme to the other, according to the point of view adopted.
I have here statements of policy and resolutions adopted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in 1958 and 1959, relating, so to speak, to the old age pensions act and more directly to government annuities which, according to the chambers of commerce, should be taken into account. Here is what we read, among other things:
Government annuities
WHEREAS at the time when Canadian government annuities were instituted, old age pension was not in force in Canada, and it was desirable that Canadians be helped in saving money for their old age; WHEREAS since the coming into force of the old age pension act a certain protection is assured; WHEREAS old age pensions are costing the government large sums of money and, on the other hand, government annuities call for annual disbursements which tend to increase and which are a further burden upon the taxpayers, while being of benefit to only a small part of the population which, in any case, is entitled to old age pensions;
Be it therefore resolved that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce urges the federal government:
1.	To cease all advertising of government annuities, and to dismiss or transfer the personnel employed for that purpose.
2.	To discontinue group annuities.
Of course, that is an opinion with which I do not entirely agree, but which was expressed by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. That body would like government annuities to be discontinued believing that the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act, now in force, adequately protect our senior citizens.
Several other opinions which I do not necessarily support were also expressed on this matter but there is one, among others,

which was expressed, in February 1959, by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce about social measures coming under the government, and whose benefits extend to all of Canada. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the record that opinion which I find on page 11 of the brief submitted by the Chamber of Commons. Here it is:
(Text):
Social welfare.
In the field of social welfare the chamber believes that a careful distinction must be drawn between what is socially desirable as an ultimate aim and what can be achieved without damaging the system that makes our social welfare advances possible. Any additions to the already expensive welfare programs should be carefully assessed, not only with regard to their initial costs, but also with regard to their foreseeable growth and supplementary requirements over the years. In principle, the chamber believes that any additional welfare expenditures should be delayed until the full impact of present commitments can be assessed. Individuals should be encouraged to make every effort to provide for their own future and protect themselves against ordinary hazards.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, the latter view as expressed to the ministers of finance and of national revenue in February 1959 is somewhat at variance with the view I quoted a moment ago, which is also part of resolutions and policies approved by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and which calls, so to speak, for the abolition of government annuities on the grounds that the old age security act and the old age assistance act now take care of the needs of older people when they have to retire.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, there are other problems related to this matter of pensions, for instance the problem of providing employment for older workers, namely those who have reached the age of 60 or 65, or other people who are refused jobs by reason of their age. It has been found that a good many citizens between 60 and 65 years of age were deprived of any form of social assistance because of the fact that they could not get old age assistance pensions and were not eligible for the old age security pension. Campaigns have been launched in that connection by various organizations, such as the Chambers of Commerce, labour unions and even the Department of Labour, to encourage employers to continue employing such people-

If it would be fair for the chamber of commerce to decide the old age pensioners' pensions, would it not be equally fair for the old age pensioners to decide the profits of the chamber of commerce?

each and fairness to all. I do not share the view, nor does the Conservative party, of those who are opposed to all forms of social justice. Individuals and groups will disagree, of course, as to what is fair to them from their own special viewpoint. It is the duty of government to reconcile these views in the general interest and to take action to achieve for all Canadians the highest measure of social justice within the resources of the nation."
In keeping with this concept, social justice payments to individual Canadians in every category of assistance have increased substantially since 1956-57.
In the three major categories of old age pensions, family allowances and unemployment insurance, the estimated increase for the current year compared with the last year of the Liberals is 50 per cent- from about $1 billion to $1] billion.
And it will probably exceed this amount by the end of this year.
Old age pension payments are up in these years from $379 million to $578 million, largely due to the action of the present government in increasing the pension from $46 to $55 per month.
Of course, other measures were passed by the Conservative government; but only old age pensions are referred to here.
As far as old age pensions and the proposed amendment are concerned, I must say that many of my constituents have written urging that those pensions be tied to the cost of living and suggesting that they be paid from age 60.
All those representations are surely legitimate, especially if we consider that old age pensioners have worked hard for the greatness of this country, and that they now need increased assistance, apart from the fact that the medical care needed by many of them is more expensive. In fact, the cost of medical care has increased a great deal in the last few years.
I trust that the present government which, in the past, has shown its understanding of this problem and which, as I said earlier, and as the hon. member for Essex East himself mentioned, has increased old age pensions from $46 to $55 a month, will take these matters under consideration and will find an answer to those problems, so that our senior citizens may live happier in their old age and be in a position to pay for the medical care they need. As I have pointed out, there are unquestionably categories of persons who need a pension at a certain age, and I am sure that the present government will see to it.
