Mr. Speaker, although I realize it is within the rules for an amendment to be moved to the motion to go into supply in the way in which it was done today, I feel it is very

unfair to hon. members to have this amendment moved without any notice and without an opportunity to prepare to speak on this particular subject.
This is a matter that is very much in the minds of all hon. members, because the plight of our senior citizens is always in our thoughts. I listened carefully to the speech made by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin). One of the difficulties with regard to this amendment is the setting of the exact figure of $75 a month to which old age pensions should be raised. I listened to hear what the hon. member for Timiskaming had to say about it. He did mention that $75 may be a reasonable figure. He also went on to say that some other figure might be a reasonable one. This is the difficulty in which I find myself, and I am sure all other hon. members are in the same position. We must have some guide, something on which the amount of pension shall be fixed, rather than picking out of the air a figure such as $75 a month, which is quite an increase over the present figure.
When he was speaking about this matter the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said that when his government was in power it did not give increases such as the Conservative government gave; he also said it did not even promise any. I think the effect of his speech is that the Liberal government did not even consider any type of plan except the one they introduced in 1957, just prior to the federal election, when they gave an increase for political purposes, the very thing the hon. member for Essex East was trying to accuse the government of this morning.
No doubt the amendment is one that meets with universal approval in principle. The welfare of our own people is something that we must all consider from time to time. It is not sufficient, as has been mentioned, just to think of it at election time and give something in the nature of an increase which might be considered as a vote-getting proposition.
As has been mentioned, the Clark report was brought in after considerable investigation of the systems which are in existence in the United States in regard to old age security and social security generally. I think it is quite unfair to say that the present government promised that when they obtained power they would adopt the United States system. I am positive that no one could take any such meaning from any speeches made during the election campaign. We did not say that. I am sure no one said that if elected this government would bring in the same system that exists in the United States. However, the government did say that that system had a lot of merit and that it would be studied. That study has been made and a report has been brought in. Apparently it has not yet

been implemented, but it does form the basis of such plans as the government may have for an over-all social security plan in this country.
While it is difficult to wait, yet I think we are bound to wait until all the factors have been considered before we say that the old age pension should be $75 a month, and just leave it at that. There must be some guidance, something to assist us in arriving at such a formula.
In connection with the pension of $55 a month which was brought in in 1957, at that time the vast majority of the old people of Canada felt that this pension allowance was quite sufficient, and they were very happy with it. Admittedly, in different parts of the country it affects people differently. A good many of the people in the rural sections of the country, such as Parry Sound-Muskoka which I represent, if they are retired with their own homes and have reasonable municipal taxes, are quite capable of getting along on $110 a month for groceries and clothing. A good many people find this to be quite adequate and they have so expressed themselves to me on many occasions.
On the other hand, there are people in other areas who find it impossible to get along on that amount. The people in the urban areas find that they can hardly rent premises at that figure, and certainly they have very little for rent and food unless they happen to own their own homes. Therefore it is not an easy thing to fix an amount which will be suitable for everyone. But I do say that in 1957 the vast majority of the people of this country felt that $55 a month was sufficient. I am not suggesting that it is sufficient today.
I have always felt that pensions for the old people should be fixed on the basis of the consumer price index or, as we call it, the cost of living index. The cost of living index has been reasonably stable over the past few years, yet it is important that we consider it. Therefore over the noon hour I made some inquiries about the cost of living index over the past few years to see what we ought to do in this house with reference to increasing the old age pension.
I have stated on several occasions that I felt any increases to be given should be tied to the consumer price index, so that if prices and the cost of living go up the old age pensioner will have his pension increased a similar amount. As we all know, the consumer price index covers a large number of factors. The figures I have obtained are for the over-all cost of living index as published by the dominion bureau of statistics, which I think is the most reliable index we can use.
Old Age Pensions
In June, 1956 the consumer price index in Canada stood at 117.8. As all hon. members know, this is based on an index of 100 which was re-established in 1949. From June, 1956 to June, 1957 it showed a very substantial increase to 121.6. This was an increase of nearly four points in the one year. I do not think it has any relation whatsoever to the matter, but it was the last year of the Liberal administration. Then in June of 1958 the index took another jump and increased to 125.1.
In the following year, 1959, it hardly moved, rising from 125.1 to 125.9. The increase from 1958 to 1959 was very slight. The dominion bureau of statistics has just issued the current figure in a release dated July 8, 1960. We find that for June of this year the over-all consumer price index stood at 127.6, or an increase of little over 1J points. It is stated in the release respecting the June consumer price index that the household operation index declined fractionally from May to June, but that in the over-all picture there was an increase of 0.2 per cent.
Taking these figures, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to work out what we should do on this basis. In other words, where would the rate of pension now stand if it were increased in proportion to the cost of living index? Taking the June, 1957 pension figure at $55, the consumer price index at that time was 121.6, and if an escalator clause had been inserted at that time the old age pension would now be $57.75 on the basis of the June, 1960 consumer price index of 127.6. In other words there would have been an increase of $2.75 in the amount of the pension payable each month.

Would the hon.
member permit a question?
Certainly.
On the basis of the argument the hon. member is developing now, does the hon. member think the amount of $55 granted in 1957 was adequate for old age pensioners at that time?

I thought I had stated what my view was in my earlier remarks. I said that in some cases it was quite adequate and in others it was not, depending on the location in which the old age pensioner lived.

It would be all right for
former prime minister St. Laurent.

In suggesting that the amount would now be $57.75 I want to make it very clear that I am not proposing we should raise the pension today to $57.75. This is merely a comparison to indicate that the figure of $75 bears no relation whatsoever to the amount of the pension in 1957. Perhaps

Old Age Pensions
the figure of $55 was inadequate in certain cases, but if we use that as a basis the pension certainly would not have risen as high as $75 at this time.
I have some difficulty in opposing the amendement today because of the rather unfortunate experience of a former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, who also based an increase on a nice mathematical calculation which resulted in an increase of $6, and which turned out to be a most unfortunate sum of money and a most unsatisfactory adjustment. However, I am saying that the tying of the cost of living index to the pension is something that would be most desirable.
To deal with the amendment itself, I believe it is classed as a non-confidence motion. That is the only way I can see it at the moment. It is an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply, and in my view it is put forward as a want of confidence amendment. I admit right away that I find myself in a difficult position, and I have no doubt in the world that it exactly what the hon. member for Timmins had in mind when he proposed the amendment, not only with respect to myself but a good many other people. Nevertheless, that is the situation; he has put me on the spot along with a good many other members.
If I want to embarrass the government I do not have to go to that length.

I was merely suggesting that this was an effort to embarrass some hon. members. I feel that the old age pension question has not been satisfactorily settled yet. That is my view of the matter. I think the pension must be adjusted from time to time, and that the present rate of $55 must be reconsidered. The reason I am embarrassed is that I may have to vote against an amendment to increase the pension to $75 when such a move in other circumstances might be worthy of consideration. However, in my opinion the arbitrary setting of a figure of $75 with no previous consideration of the matter except what may be given today is not satisfactory. The matter has not been discussed previously this session. It was not brought up on the minister's estimates, and I believe that the amendment is hastily conceived.

You never even got started.

-I regret this incident, since it would never be my intention to interfere with the designs of the whip in any material way. However, you will recall that I did rise this morning, before the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I did address the Chair. After lunch I was a bit uncertain about my position, so I wrote a note to Mr. Speaker, who told me I was right after the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). It was for this reason I got up just now and addressed the Chair. I listened, as I said, very attentively to the representative of the C.C.F. group who introduced this amendment, as well as to the hon. member for Essex East. I could see nothing in what they said, with one possible exception, that was not in strict conformity with the solemn promises we officially made during the 1957 and 1958 elections.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a few remarks I made on January 16, 1956, when I first spoke in this house. I made a very definite and very lengthy statement at that time to the effect that pensions ought to be granted at 65 years of age and ought to be increased to $60 per month. This was in 1956. It must be remembered that at that time the pension was $40 per month. That was the first time I made a speech in the house, having only recently been elected. I came here at that time having very fresh in my mind the pleas of hundreds of thousands of senior citizens, not only in my riding but in all parts of Canada, to the effect that they simply could not get along on $40 per month. They cannot get along now on $55 per month, Mr. Speaker.
If I may be permitted, I should like to quote from page 175 of Hansard, volume 1, 1956. I said this:
Nothing stifles initiative and the joy of living so much as the realization that once you reach age 65 your services will no longer be in demand ...
The general tendency within our industries is to enforce compulsory retirement at age 65. This affects not only the health of those who have to retire, but also the entire economy of the country.
Then on the same page I said:
We should protect our citizens who, after a long life of hard work, are anxious to work in order to retain their health and happiness. We must afford them the opportunity of taking up another occupation, if their health is adequate, and if they are anxious to continue to work. I am not claiming that

they should continue in the same line of work as the one in which they were engaged throughout their life
They should be encouraged and given an opportunity to become occupied in a line of work that would give them something useful to do and permit them to make a contribution to the economic welfare of Canada. This is the plight in which so many of our senior citizens find themselves on reaching the age of 65. Their services are no longer required. When I made these few remarks in 1956 I said this:
Where would the Liberal party be today had the Prime Minister been forced to retire at 65, along with the other members of his cabinet?
If what is true of government and what is true of industry were applied right across the country, then we would be confronted with a situation throughout this country in which people reaching the age of 65 would be told to go home, that their years of usefulness were over. In some cases, in an ever-increasing number of cases, they are given a pension to which they contributed during their years of employment.
However, Mr. Speaker, the point I wish to make is that this pension is not adequate, in the first place, and in the second place this is a trend that should be abated. It is a trend that should be discouraged by every possible means. People should be given the opportunity of continuing to make the contribution they feel capable of making throughout the useful years of their lives. The age of 65 should not be arbitrarily set as the retirement age. I know that the setting of that age goes back to the time of Bismark, who when they introduced social security in 1885 in Germany adopted the age of 65 as the age at which the pension should be paid. There was no trend at that time which indicated that should be the age at which people should retire.
Of course these people are forced to retire, and they are given a small pension. If these people, throughout their lives, have had the courage to save a few dollars, to own a house, acquire a little bit of real estate or place a few dollars in investments, they are denied a pension because of the means test. I said in 1956, as recorded on the same page of Hansard:
I cannot understand the thinking of the Liberal party leaders as regards the means test.
I cannot understand why we are not taking steps, and have not taken steps, to abolish the means test for a pension at age 65. Why punish a person because he has had the courage to save a few dollars? Why penalize a person because he has provided, to some extent, for his future? Why is it that

Old Age Pensions
you have to be poor to get the old age pension at 65, and be very careful to remain poor in order to keep it? If you go to work, as happens in ridings such as mine where summer employment is more readily available than winter employment and is of a less strenuous nature, then the next thing you know you get a letter saying that your pension has been eliminated, cut, cancelled or reduced, sometimes for a period of six months or more. This happens when a pensioner earns a little more than he is permitted to earn. In other words, these old age pensioners are forced to remain poor. They are prevented from improving their standard of living and they are penalized because of this means test.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that this is a good occasion indeed upon which to bring to the attention of this house the iniquitous results of this means test which affects so many of our people. If the pensions which people received from their former employers were sufficient to permit them to enjoy a decent life, then the situation might be different. However, in ridings such as mine there are no pensions from employers at age 65, in most cases. A man is forced to stop working at one job, but he is not given an opportunity to work anywhere else. Even our provincial governments and our federal government have fallen into the habit of putting people into that category. A man cannot even become a fish warden on the Restigouche river during the summer months if he is over 65 years of age. A man is penalized, therefore; he is caught in a vise. The pendulum has swung and it has swung in a way that has hurt our senior citizens.
I feel that although the second point is of importance, the means test was never designed to penalize a man or prevent him from improving his standard of living or from earning a few dollars that might permit him to live more decently. But if the means test is important, so is the attitude we in this group took throughout the years with regard to old age pensions. I can recall that in 1929 the Conservative party in New Brunswick had in its platform the implementation of old age pensions. The party spent four years in office and did not carry out that promise because they felt the government could not afford to do so. Of course they lost the election, or they did not lose it so much as they gave it away in the very same manner that the Flemming government just lost in New Brunswick; they gave the election away.
As our attitude has crystallized over the years we have been consistently in favour

not only of old age pensions but of increasing them to the point where people in their older years would be permitted to live decently. I can assure you that among the members of the old opposition-and we were in the opposition for a good many years-who were the most eloquent and most ardent advocates of better treatment for our senior citizens, who took an interest in their plight and who carried on such a vigorous struggle to make sure that they received the consideration that this government should have given them, was none other than the present Prime Minister of Canada. Let us not forget that fact.
But we came to the people in 1958, and there is no question in my mind about this fact. I know that I went to my riding and I read the promises. I repeated them, I spoke about them and probably I even signed them. I refer to the promises that the hon. member for Essex East recited this morning. There was no question in my mind then but that we had undertaken them officially. This was not a promise caught up by some candidate, as may have been the case in some instances. This was an official solemn obligation on the part of this government and this party to implement the same system of social security, over and above the present system, that existed in the United States. There was no doubt in my mind at that time that that was the official position of the party. I certainly made it one of the important things in the campaign I waged in my riding of Resti-gouche-Madawaska. There is no person in that riding now who is not keenly aware of the fact that during the past one and a half years we have more or less sidetracked that extremely important obligation that we accepted on behalf of this party toward the Canadian people.
As to this system of social security as it has existed in the United States, may I say this. I realize that in order to implement this system and replace the present one would result in injustice, would create havoc and would be detrimental to the interests of the people. But this was not a system to replace the one in existence. This was a system that was to be implemented in addition to and over and above the present system of old age pensions which were to be increased as they were increased.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the hour is getting late. I feel that this system of survivor benefits, the same system as that which exists in the United States, must be implemented in Canada now. I contend that it should have been implemented previously, but I say that it must be implemented now. I realize that this system, being a contributory one, will

have more popular appeal in the highly industrialized areas of Canada and possibly not as much appeal and possibly not as much ability to contribute in areas such as mine where the population is to a great extent rural.
I understand that the only reason that program has not been implemented up to now is that the average wages in Canada are something like 30 per cent less than the average wages in the United States. But let us not forget this fact. The average wages in New Brunswick are 30 per cent less than the average wages in Canada as a whole. You can therefore realize the position in which our people find themselves. By and large our people are unable to contribute to the welfare of their fathers and mothers. They are unable to adequately supplement the pensions of $55 a month that are now being paid.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that until such time as we decide to take the bull by the horns and implement this system of social security as it exists in the United States, making allowances for areas such as mine where people do not earn enough money to contribute to it, we should give careful consideration to this motion. It is impossible to get along on $55 a month. I do not care where you come from in this country; that is the situation.
I remember that in the old days Mr. John Blackmore brought into the house a set of figures furnished by the department of statistics, which gave the minimum required by an old person or an elderly person to get along. Here are the figures which were given, more or less; there may be some little variance. It was found that a person could not get along on less than $30 a month for food. That is allowing only 33 cents a meal, which I understand is less than we allow for our prisoners. You had to expect to pay $20 a month for rent. That was only $5 a week, or less than a dollar a day. Those figures were supplied by the department of statistics. The person was expected to give at least $3 a month to the church. The amount of a $7 a month was allowed for clothes, $10 a month for recreation and $5 for transportation. As I add those figures up, they come to $75.
I feel that $75 a month is a realistic amount. I do not think this government will very soon carry out its obligation to put into effect the same or almost the same social security system as that which is in existence in the United States. I am not thinking about any election in the past and I am not thinking about any election to come. I am thinking of the old people of this country, the senior
Old Age Pensions
citizens, not only in my riding but throughout all of Canada. I say that the time has come to give this question the consideration it merits.
We increased the pension to $55 a month, and then we seemed to develop the feeling that we had taken the load off our shoulders and that we were not obliged to think about it again. Of course that increase was welcome. However, there are very few people in this country who will say that it was adequate.
Who are we trying to help, or who are we helping? In giving due consideration to and in doing justice toward the senior citizens of this country we are helping all the people of this country and all the citizens. We are helping our young men and women. We are helping the people of middle age. We are helping all our people to shoulder the burden of responsibility to their parents. Who in this house can oppose this motion? I say, Mr. Speaker, that this motion is long overdue and should be passed.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment moved by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) has given the house an opportunity to discuss one of the most important questions that could come before us, namely the question of old age pensions. It is unfortunate that throughout the course of this discussion it has not been possible for the minister of the government directly concerned with this matter, namely the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to be here. Perhaps he is on business of public importance elsewhere. I think it is also unfortunate that the Minister of Finance, who is equally concerned, has not found it possible to be in the house this afternoon during the discussion. I say this is an important question. Our position with regard to it has been put to the house by the hon. member for Essex East, who has himself done so much for social security in this country.
As a responsible official opposition we do not ignore the relationship between social security and financial and economic resources. We know that no government that is responsible in the economic as well as the political sense of the word can do everything. We know that developing social security schemes must be related to the resources of the nation because there is only one way in which these schemes can be financed, namely by us as citizens of the country. So we on this side do not ignore that aspect of the question and we never have as a party in the past.
Over the years, in this progress toward better social security in this country, when

Old Age Pensions
Liberal governments were in power the progress was always made in a way which rec-conciled essental social progress with fiscal and economic requirements. I noticed this morning when the hon. member for Timmins introduced this amendment that it referred to a specific sum, $75 a month. At one stage, although it was somewhat confusing, he indicated that he was not wedded to any particular amount, and that he thought perhaps $75 a month at this time and in present circumstances might be too high. He will correct me if I misquote him, but I do recall him saying that. The fact remains-
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, was the Leader of the Opposition referring to me?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I beg the hon. member's pardon; it was the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters). The fact remains, however, that we do have in this amendment the figure of $75 a month.
We also recognize, while keeping in mind economic and fiscal considerations, that there are social considerations which are equally important, indeed more important, than fiscal consideration. We know that pension schemes and pension levels and social security programs generally can never be fixed but that they have to be adjusted and changes made as conditions in the country change.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear to us, as I am sure it is clear to every hon. member of this house, that the claims of old age pensioners must be very high on the list of priorities when we are considering what more we can do in developing schemes for responsible social security and social progress.
The government itself has given certain definite and specific assurances in this field. We have also been told more than once by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) that when an assurance is given by the prime minister of this country, that assurance means something and will lie kept. The Prime Minister himself emphasized that the other day. In this particular field the assurances are specific. Some of them were mentioned this morning, and I will quote one given by the Prime Minister on April 25, 1957 when beginning the election campaign. As reported by the Canadian Press he said:
As for social security-pensions, veterans payments and the like-the increases announced in last month's federal budget were "meagre and niggardly". A Conservative government would set payments high enough to meet needs...
The concept of pensions then, as expressed by the present Prime Minister, was the concept of need. The pensions would be set high enough, he said, to meet needs. He did not end there. Having established what the need

was for pensions, and I admit that was done shortly after the government took office, and having established it at the figure of $55 a month, the Prime Minister further said on April 25, 1957:
A Conservative government would set payments high enough to meet needs and subsequent adjustments to living costs and increases in national productivity.
So first of all they were going to establish what the need was, and they did establish it at $55. Subsequently they would make adjustments to living costs and increases in national productivity. That was in 1957, and there have been increases in living costs and in national productivity since that time. That was surely a specific, definite assurance, and presumably it was meant to be kept. But it has not been kept.
Mr. Speaker, this motion is an opportunity for the Prime Minister to indicate whether he wishes to take advantage of this situation in order to reaffirm this assurance which he gave in 1957.
He gave another assurance in 1958 which has already been referred to. When opening the campaign he pledged, on February 12, 1958:
We will bring about in Canada a sound and effective contributory social security plan-
And I emphasized these words.
-over and above that which already exists.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are the three assurances which the Prime Minister of this country gave and by which he is bound. First of all, that he would establish the old age pension scheme on the basis of need; second, that having established the need he would adjust pensions to take care of the increase in the cost of living and the growth of national productivity; and third, that he would add to these schemes a contributory scheme over and above what has been provided in the way of universal old age pensions. As the hon. member for Essex East said, he made great play with this latter assurance. A commission was set up to tell us how it could be done, and the report of the commission has been in the hands of the government for two years and is still being considered.
Mr. Speaker, I have said that we are unable to accept the amendment, which relates the increase to a specific amount, $75 a month, without condition, without reservation, without qualification. I propose to move an amendment to the amendment which will establish the position of our own party in regard to this and related matters on a basis -and I emphasize this-which has already been laid down in our party platform. This amendment embodies the assurances which

we as a party have already given and by which we will stand, and which in due course we will implement.
This amendment to the amendment reads as follows. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill):
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after the word "provide" and the substitution therefor of the following words:
"in co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships endured by the recipients of old age security and old age assistance; to extend old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age; for the vesting of benefits in industrial pensions plans; and for a national contributory pension scheme, co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security based on federal government contributions, as well as on contributions of employees, employers, and self-employed."
The original amendment as amended would then read:
That in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide, in co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships endured by the recipients of old age security and old age assistance; to extend old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age; for the vesting of benefits in industrial pensions plans; and for a national contributory pension scheme, co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security based on federal government contributions, as well as on contributions of employees, employers, and self-employed.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that everyone in the House of Commons would like to see the old age pension and other pensions increased. I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and gathered that they are wholeheartedly in support of increased pensions. I find it difficult, however, to reconcile their words of today with their actions of the past because when they were in a position to do these things they simply did not do them.
We have heard a lot about the great social measures that the previous government brought in. I should like to put on the record some of the things the Conservative government has done in the past three years because I believe that no government in Canada has ever laid as great emphasis on human needs as this government has. I feel sure that if the Conservative party had not been elected in 1957 our older citizens would still be receiving a pension of $46 a month. It was not until the Conservatives formed the government that the pension was raised to $55 a month. It was not until the Conservatives formed the government that an injustice was removed which made it necessary that people should have lived in Canada for 20 years before they were eligible for any pension. The domicile period was reduced to 10 years by the Conservative government. It was not until the Conservatives formed the government that another injustice was wiped out through this government abolishing the regulation which provided that old age pensioners had to live in Canada in order to be eligible for the pension. These are just a few of the measures we have introduced to date, a few of the step by step improvements that this government has brought about in our social measures.
It is time for another.

We are getting there. In my constituency of York-Humber there are

Old Age Pensions
hundreds of old age pensioners. I know how much they appreciate these improvements. I know they would appreciate receiving $75 a month, too, and I sincerely hope we can raise the old age pension in the not too distant future.
Canadians are responsible people, Mr. Speaker. They know that we cannot take on welfare measures beyond our means. I believe there are approximately 875,000 old age pensioners in Canada today and this number is increasing all the time as longevity increases. The socialists who have been rejected again and again by the Canadian people now pull out of their hat the figure of $75 a month. Why $75 a month? I have here a brief from the national old age pensioners' federation and they suggest $85 a month payable without a means test to all citizens on reaching age 65. Why not $85? Or better still, why not a nice round figure like $100 a month? It is so easy for the socialists to introduce these irresponsible amendments knowing that they will never have to meet the problem of the heavy expenditures involved. The socialists talk about free hospitalization, free medical care, free pensions, free pie in the sky. Of course, it is downright dishonest on their part to make these irrational statements because nothing is free. Somebody has to pay for all these things and it is not governments that pay for them. Governments do not have money and so it is the taxpayers who pay for them.
From the province of Saskatchewan we have heard a lot about free medical care. The government of Saskatchewan certainly has no money to provide free medical care except what they take from the unfortunate taxpayers. It is the duty of responsible governments to try and assess how far Canada can go in its social welfare. I believe that responsible governments must gear social welfare to our economic capacity.
The question has come up today, do we want a system such as the United States has or do we want a combination of our system and of the United States personal contributory system? It took the United States 22 years to build up a fund that pays a minimum of $33 a month. If we scrap our system, how long would it take before we could build up a sound fund that would pay $55 a month? It seems to me that our $55 a month for everyone is much fairer than the United States system. Under our system you cannot get higher pensions nor can you get lower pensions. Theirs is a system whereby the rich get richer, that is higher pensions, and the poor get poorer, or lower pensions, which are based on the amount of the contribution

through the productive years. I think our system under which everybody gets the same is the best one.
Then, the dream of having our system plus the contributory system I think is a good one. I hope in time that we have it, but I am looking into the distant future because it will take many years to build up a sound contributory fund; and looking into the near future I also hope that we can raise the old age pension in a responsible and sound way.

Mr. Speaker I rise to express my opposition to the subamendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). As I read his subamendment he wants to eliminate a definite expression of opinion on the part of the house that we believe the government ought to give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide for an increase to $75 a month in old age pensions. He has replaced that with the wish that the house might express its opinion in favour of a long list of platitudes. He does not want the house to express an opinion that our senior citizens ought to receive a minimum of at least $75 a month. I did not hear him use the words but I imagine he regards our proposal as irresponsible. I am advised that the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) indicated that our proposal might be irresponsible, but we have made an estimate of what the cost might be, and the gross expense of implementing our amendment and enabling all pensioners to receive $75 a month instead of $55 a month that they now get would mean an added burden to the treasury of a little bit more than $200 million a year. When we recall that this year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is paying $249,728,162 more in interest on the public debt than was paid in the financial year ended March 31, 1957; when we consider that added increase in interest payments made by the federal government on its obligations, I think that a gross expenditure of a little more than $200 million in order to give reasonable equity to our senior citizens is not beyond the capacity of our nation to bear.
I hold in my hand the Bible which I obtained from the table and I note that in Exodus, chapter 20, verse 12, it says:
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God glveth thee.
I feel that if we as a society deny to our fathers and mothers a standard of living that is equal to ours we are not obeying the commandment that was given to mankind many long years ago. I see no reason why in our society those who are willing to work, but

because of factors beyond their control are unable to work, ought not to share and to have the same standard of living as the members of our society who are able to earn a regular monthly wage. I believe that the motion moved by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) ought not to be denied passage by the house, and that we ought to reject this attempt on the part of the Liberal party to water down the amendment with platitudes, many of which may be acceptable but which, however, in effect would express the opinion that we ought not to commit ourselves to a minimum income of $75 a month for our elderly citizens.
I am rather amazed at the words used in the subamendment submitted by the Leader of the Opposition. To begin with, he used the words "in co-operation with the provinces". I would have hoped that he would explain that approach a little more clearly than he did. Exactly what does he mean, because we now have an old age pension that is paid to all Canadians as Canadians. The pension that we are now paying has nothing to do with the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Why the Leader of the Opposition wants to re-introduce the co-operation of the other levels of government in this regard I do not understand except, and in this I relate it to what immediately follows, that he wishes to have increases in the old age pension only to meet special hardships. Is the Liberal party now attempting to re-introduce the means test into the old age pension? The only interpretation I can place on this wording is that the Liberals are perfectly willing to pay $55 a month to each and every Canadian who has reached the ripe old age of 70. However, they are unwilling to grant any more than $55 unless the proposed recipient can plead a special hardship.
Then in the subamendment offered by the Leader of the Opposition there is an indication that the increase ought to be granted only if-and I read this into it-a contribution is made by the provincial authorities. This is a negation of the intent of our amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply. Our amendment means that the federal authorities should, in the same way that they now assume the obligation to pay $55 a month, assume the obligation to pay not $55 but $75 a month to every eligible Canadian.
I had reference to platitudes before and in that regard I should like to consider the amendment to the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. He refers to extending old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age. We have no fault to find with that. He also refers to
Old Age Pensions
the vesting of benefits in industrial pension plans. Obviously the Leader of the Opposition has at long last heard of the numerous complaints of unions with regard to the vesting of industrial pension plans and has thrown in that point so as not to overlook it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It has been in our program for two years.

He also refers to a national contributory pension scheme. I have always understood that all Canadians who pay income tax are making a contribution to old age pensions and that we already have a contributory basis. For the Leader of the Opposition to call now for a contributory pension scheme without further elaboration seems rather meaningless because in our view we now have such a scheme. In the amendment to the amendment he has added the words, "co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security based on federal government contributions, as well as on contributions of employees, employers and self-employed". If the Leader of the Opposition means that he is advocating a portable pension plan, naturally we are all in agreement. However, I should like to ask him why he does not ask for a portable pension plan in his amendment. Why does he have to use all these words which merely confuse the issue?
We believe that the Canadian economy has the ability to pay the increase of $200 million required to implement our plan. Let us never forget that this would not be the net cost to the country because much of this money would be returned to the Minister of Finance by way of income tax, sales tax and all kinds of other levies. I would risk a guess that at least $80 million of the $200 million odd required to implement our plan would be returned to various levels of government in one way or another. Therefore the net cost to government would be only slightly in excess of $100 million.
Mention was made that our amendment has to be related to the resources of the nation. In our opinion the resources of the nation are adequate and the resources of any nation should always be adequate to ensure a standard of living to fathers and mothers at least equal to our own. In my view the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timmins represents one effort to restore a little equity to the pioneers of our nation.
Much has been made of the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). Members of the Liberal party seem to think that he indicated that $75 might be too high.

Old Age Pensions
I believe that they have completely misinterpreted and misunderstood the hon. member for Timiskaming. All he was arguing was that the income of Canada's senior citizens should be tied to the cost of living and that when the cost of living rises their income should also rise. It may well be that if the cost of living declines their income should decline as well. I do not think any of Canada's elder citizens would find fault with that argument. However, the Liberals have attempted to misinterpret the hon. member's remarks as indicating that there may be one member in our group who is of the opinion that in this day and age $75 a month may be unduly high.
The Liberals would like to indicate their support for a substantial increase. All I will do is refer readers of Hansard to the Liberal interpretation of what a substantial increase means. In their view an increase from $40 to $46 a month represents a substantial increase. The Liberals are making an effort to get themselves off the hook. They do not want to commit themselves to a specific figure or to be realistic. As the Liberals have always done, they want to hand out charity to our elder Canadians under the pressure of elections. They do not want to grant equity. We in this group demand that those who have founded and been responsible for the building of our nation be granted equitable treatment and our proposal for the payment of $75 a month is only one means of obtaining equity for them.

Mr. Speaker, I was attending the bill of rights committee when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) moved the amendment to the

amendment. I understand he indicated at that time that the official opposition would oppose the amendment moved by the C.C.F. party.
I merely wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I very much regret the position that has been taken by the Liberal party. We gave consideration, in drafting our amendment, to making it rather broad and including many things within it. However, I feel, from the standpoint of the opposition, it is much more effective to move a simple, concise amendment that leaves no room for argument as to where the party moving it stands. We think our amendment is in this category. It calls for a very simple act by the government, namely considering an increase in the old age pension of $20 per month. I think that in view of the cost of living and in view of the production of which Canada is capable, this is a reasonable proposition. Certainly the additional call on our resources that would flow from an increase of $20 a month would not be impossible to meet because all across the country today we have widespread unemployment.
The Liberal party complains about unemployment. They ask the government to act on unemployment. I submit that one of the best actions the government could take to help relieve the unemployment situation would be to put some very badly needed purchasing power into the hands of people receiving old age pensions. This, in turn, would increase employment in our country. In 1957 the Liberals increased the old age pension by $6 per month. I understand that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)-I do not want to misquote him-said that if we had asked for a pension of $65 a month they would have given favourable consideration to that proposition. I feel that the Liberal party, more than any other party in Canada, should know the results that flow from recognizing the principle that an increase is necessary, and bringing in an inadequate increase.
In 1957, before that election, no one would argue that the old people of this country did not need an increase in their pension. However, when the Liberal party brought in an increase amounting to a miserable $6, an amount which, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out was just 20 cents a day, a couple of cups of coffee a day, they did something which, more than any other single thing, assured that after the election they would transfer from the right of the Speaker to the left of the Speaker.

speechtext:

*-In co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships endured by the recipients of old age security and old age assistance;-[DOT]
This, Mr. Speaker, amounts to nothing more than bringing back the means test by a backdoor method to the old age security pensioners. We felt that a step forward had been taken by removing the means test so that every Canadian, no matter what his or her status, on reaching the age of 70 would be entitled to a pension of a certain amount. The Liberal subamendment would stigmatize the people of this country who are now in receipt of old age security and who are in a special position of hardship. I feel that would be a retrograde step and one that parliament should not endorse at this time.

They have placed in the subamendment many things that we have advocated for many years and we would be prepared to support as a definite proposition. However, we are not prepared to support this gobbledy-gook type amendment which removes the

effect of our own amendment which was clear and precise. It was to help the old age pensioners of this country. We said the old people of this country need help, but the Liberal party says, do not help them now; let us go on this long, tortuous course and try to get the co-operation of the provinces to do all manner of things as listed in this subamendment.
My hon. friend knows that that is not the case.

Mr. Speaker, I think without question the record of this government in the security field has been the best of any government since confederation. I think all hon. members of the house will agree with that statement. I think that all you have to do is to look at the record. The government has increased the old age pension. In 1956-57 the amount was $379 million; in 1959 we paid out $578 million or $200 million of an increase over the previous government.
In old age security alone?
In pensions to our senior citizens who qualify.
No.

Oh, yes. In the field of social security I want to refer to this point. We have given over $100 million more for mothers' and children's allowances across Canada, making a total in those two fields alone, going into the homes of Canada where it was needed, of over $300 million.
Not in mothers' allowances.

In my capacity as a physician I have seen the great good that has been done by this increase since this present government has come into power. It is an interesting fact to note that here is conversion. I remember so well that the previous government explained that $46 was all the 
economy of the state would stand. I have also read some articles from the province of Saskatchewan and I note that Dr. James Forrester made the statement out there in Saskatoon in an address a couple of months ago that it is always possible for welfare costs to exceed the value of the gross national product, which would end in a breakdown of all our social security measures. I think those are fundamentals that we must keep in mind in any field of taxation.
I am sure there is no one in this house who for one minute would deny the old people all that they have coming to them in their declining years for their comfort and their security. But I am also equally sure that there are other fields in which we need expansion just as badly as we need this increase. I refer particularly to those cases of people in the sixties and seventies who are obliged to go to hospitals and are placed in general hospital wings when they would be better placed in wings particularly devised for the treatment and the benefit of those people who are in the chronically ill class.
Then I also think of the person who is not acutely ill or is not sick enough to be in hospital, or even in a geriatric wing of that hospital, but who needs invalid care, and we have done very little about this matter in this country. There have been a few pilot schemes but beyond that we have done very little. I think there is a great and growing need for this and it must be more urgently considered by all levels of government. In our older age groups sickness increases by leaps and bounds. I have not heard anyone mention that in this house this afternoon except the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). Yes, I am going to give the hon. member credit. He mentioned it but he said no medical care was provided. Medical care is provided where the old age recipient is unable to pay and these people get excellent care. Not only is that the case, but this government brought in hospitalization whereby these people have their hospitalization taken care of. Yes, that is true and we brought in hospitalization and; we also provided them with drugs so that there is no old age pensioner today, who is entitled to it by lack of means, who cannot get the best treatment that is possible in this dominion of Canada. Those are things this government has done. However, there are other things that need to be done.
There are those people who, for reasons of infirmity, cannot look after themselves. There is a great and crying need across this nation for the building of homes in which these people can be looked after and in which our schemes of hospitalization would pay for them and look after them.
Why have you not done it?

What provision is made for those people that are able to work?
Will the hon. member name one in that category on whose behalf I have not spoken in this house? Will he name one? I should like to know.

Mr. Speaker, sometimes the hon. member is in the past. I want to dwell on the fact that a great many of these people have reached the age of 65. You will find them quite often welcomed into the home. They fit more easily into the home many times than do men. Often there are positions open for them that are not often open to men. It is true that they form the largest number. There are many more old age pensioners among the women than there are among the men. Dinsdale (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I think I can safely say that I have been around the house long enough to recognize what is involved in the amendment we have before us here this afternoon. As I listened to the speeches that have been made on this very important subject, the sentiments
Old Age Pensions
all pull in the direction of the senior citizens of Canada. Unfortunately, however, in speaking to the amendments to the motion to go into supply we are somewhat hamstrung by the very nature of the amendments themselves.
A member supporting this government- and several of the speakers have reviewed the social welfare progress and anticipated program of the government-confronted with these resolutions is forced to come to the conclusion that they are nothing more nor less than a want of confidence motion in this government. Having said that I think we are rather disappointed that this important subject, the situation of our senior citizens at the present time, has to be brought into focus by the amendments before the house.
The senior citizens are one of the most important segments of the population today. They have been growing in numbers in recent years. For example, in 1925 the citizens of 70 years and over in Canada represented just 5.19 per cent of the population. In 1935 that percentage had increased to 6.01 per cent, or in population figures, to 392,000. Moving forward another decade to 1945, the percentage was 6.66 and the population in figures 509,000. Then coming up to the next decade, 1955, the figure was 753,100 persons, or a population percentage of 7.98. So it can be anticipated that when we have the statistics in for the next decade there will be a similar increase in the number of citizens over the age level of 70 years constituting our population.
Because of this trend it is important that from time to time we review their position in modern society, particularly when we have social change taking place at the present rapid pace. It is unfortunate that in this House of Commons we are forced to take a political approach to these matters rather than discussing these important social welfare issues from the broad perspective of the actual social need. In speaking to the C.C.F. amendment we are faced again with the auction type of approach to the needs of our senior citizens, bidding upwards in terms of monetary compensation for the support of this growing segment of our population. This has been all too frequently the only approach to resolving the problem, the technique of buying people's votes with their own money.
Then again, in the discussion which has taken place already we have heard spokesmen from various parties boasting of the achievements of their own party in the field of social welfare services. If we were to examine the record in Canada and compare it with progress in other western countries I think we would all be forced to the conclusion that Canada was somewhat slow in

Old Age Pensions
responding to the demands of changing society from the standpoint of social welfare services.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) made the claim that his party has been responsible for every social welfare measure that is on the statute books of Canada today. I am not going to debate that point with him, but I am sure he will agree with me that all parties in every western country have responded to the demands of the changing social situation, either more slowly or more quickly, by moving toward what is known as the social welfare state. Canada has responded more slowly because we are a new country and a frontier society where the opportunities were great and where industrialization and urbanization proceeded at a slower pace.
I would not agree we were slower.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
But in response to the point the hon. member for Essex East made, let us just review the record for the moment, sticking exclusively to the approach of resolving the social problem amongst our senior citizens. Canada's first approach to the problem came around the year 1909, as I recall, and that was an annuities program designed to encourage senior citizens to make their own financial preparations for their declining years. There was no change in that program other than on the provincial level until the 1920's.
In response to the prodding of the provincial governments, in 1924, I believe it was, a committee was set up to review the whole problem. That committee reported to the house and in 1926 the House of Commons passed a bill providing for old age pensions in co-operation with the provinces. That bill was rejected by the other place and it had to come back before the house, and in 1927 it received the unanimous approval of both houses. So it will be seen that there was a rather hesitant approach to these difficulties.
It remained for the onset of the depression for Canada really to come to grips with the new trends in the new society and also to come to grips with the impact of the depression. I think the hon. member will recall, because he is a student in these matters, that it remained for a Conservative administration during the early part of the decade of the thirties really to move forward rapidly toward the social challenge of the problems arising from the new industrial society and also from the direct impact of the depression itself.

member permit a question?

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Who referred those social measures to the courts?
They were referred by the Liberal administration. These matters were outside federal competence, and it was clear that they were political devices employed by the government of the day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The matter raised by the hon. member for Essex East merely serves to underline the point I am making, that we have been very reluctant and slow to meet these problems; and in this specific case the Liberal administration tried to upset the apple cart by referring these matters to the supreme court to determine their legality.
We brought in measures which were within our constitutional competence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I believe the grounds were that the depression was no emergency.
Another interesting piece of history comes to my mind as I discuss this subject. I believe it was 1932 when the Liberal opposition of that day opposed rather strenuously the principle of assistance to the provincial governments, and that was one of the rare occasions when closure was adopted by the government in order to make it possible to provide assistance to the provincial governments to meet the challenge of the depression.
I mention these things merely to point out that down through the years the record of all parties in the house is not completely outside the pale of criticism. I do not think my friend the hon. member for Essex East wants to take undue credit for these matters. All governments in every western nation have had to respond to social realities, otherwise they would not remain in office. I make the point again that Canada's response has been somewhat slower because of the nature of our frontier society.
I could have dealt with this point at greater length but I do not think it needs any further discussion. I could have gone on to say that Liberal philosophy basically has been opposed to the exercise of the power of the state to ameliorate the social lot of citizens because it is contrary to the fundamental principle

of Liberalism and the maximum freedom of the individual but that would be getting us into a philosophical discussion.
Mill and Bentham as opposed to Mackenzie King and Franklin Roosevelt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure that my hon. friend would agree that it is only as the Liberals have adopted the Conservative philosophy which believes in exercising the power of the state to assist less privileged groups in our society that they have been able to reconcile their fundamental philosophical position with their practical position.
Coming now to the specific matter before the house I do not think that by moving the financial award to our senior citizens either up or down on the scale is going to relieve the problem that confronts us as an urban and industrial society. The number of senior citizens has grown as I have indicated. Our population of senior citizens is more than three times what it was, let us say, three decades ago. There has been almost a doubling of their numbers with each decade. If we are going to meet this challenge we have to move forward on a much broader front than in merely providing financial payments. Financial payments are only a small aspect of the whole problem of meeting social needs.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) in his interesting remarks dealt with this subject briefly. The hon. gentleman quoted scripture. He went back to old testament times and the ten commandments and referred to the basic principle of society which must be observed if society is to continue and to thrive on a healthy basis: honour thy father and thy mother. I think the hon. gentleman would be the first to agree with me that that injunction was not directed to the state but was rather directed to the family which is after all the basic unit of society.
As long as our families remain strong and healthy and as long as they are performing their proper functions that have been determined by the social process then we can be sure that society, government and all other aspects of our social life will remain sound and healthy. I think that injunction, "honour thy father and thy mother," is an indication that families in urban society find it very difficult to carry out the spirit of this important part of the decalogue because as a concomitant of the rapid social change that has been taking place we have had the breakdown of primary groups in our society. The family has tended to become disorganized

Oid Age Pensions
as is indicated by statistics of juvenile delinquency and statistics of neglect of the senior members of the family.
In addition to a break-down in the family, neighbourhood groups have tended to lose their identity. We find that one of the big problems of our senior citizens in recent times has been that of loneliness and a feeling of neglect. These things have come about as a result of the tendency of a complex civilization to push them off on the fringe of things and as a result of the break-down of neighbourhoods and community life. This has all resulted in the neglect of our senior citizens. We are not going to resolve this problem simply by an increased financial payment.
We can talk about social standards being maintained by financial payment but there are many of our senior citizens who have a substantial income, who are people of independent means, and although they have an adequate standard of living in monetary terms they do not have the standard of living which is necessary if they are going to feel they are occupying a useful place in our society.
I have long been interested in this problem. My interest emerged out of a study in which I was able to participate at the University of Chicago away back in 1948. This university has been a pioneer in the field of social sciences. At that time, immediately following world war II, in the United States as in Canada the problems of senior citizens which had been pushed aside because of the emergency of the war were being brought into sharp focus. The university conducted a major study of the problem in the great city of Chicago. I took part in that study as a humble interviewer going from door to door talking to senior citizens. I still have some of the documents we gathered at that time.
In assisting in the study I was impressed by the fact that in almost every case their problem was not a financial one but was a problem of feeling displaced in the world of modern times. It was a problem of wanting to work and of having no opportunity for employment in our industrial economy. It was a problem of health, elderly persons shut away in one room in tenement areas, cut off from their families, friends and neighbours, in ill health and without the wherewithal and without being provided by society with the facilities for relieving these difficulties. The case histories one after the other referred to this problem. They did not refer to the financial problem but rather to the problem of the loneliness and social displacement that was their lot.

Old Age Pensions
If we are going to adequately discuss this subject we cannot do so in terms of the amendments that are before the house at the present time. This is one of the basic social problems of our time. It has to be studied from the background of a broad knowledge of the difficulties and certainly we have not had an opportunity to gather that information in the short notice that has been given since the amendment was put before the house today.
I can only conclude by saying that in returning to this business of auction bidding in approaching our social welfare problems we are continuing the tendency to resolve fundamental social difficulties by political and partisan manipulation rather than by getting to the root of the matter.
Since the Conservative government took office I think we have seen a more encouraging attempt to adopt the broader approach. When the Clark commission was announced to investigate the field of old age security I thought that was a move in the right direction. The hon. members who have read the Clark report will agree with me, I think, that it contains excellent background information that will assist the federal government as well as the other levels of government, the provincial and municipal, because they have important roles to play in this whole area of social welfare, to broaden out the existing schemes in order to cope adequately with the problems that have been emphasized already in this discussion.
The attempts to deal with the broader social needs of our senior citizens are being met largely by voluntary organizations, and I think that is the way it should be. Certainly, in a free society government cannot go into a community and organize the necessary social groups in order to restore a sense of belonging to our older citizens. This is being done by second mile clubs, by twilight clubs and by all kinds of community organizations which are restoring our senior citizens to their rightful places in the social scheme of things. And then, too, provincial governments have reached out to accept the challenge in a more realistic way.
Since I come from the province of Manitoba I was encouraged just last year when the provincial government there moved forward with a very progressive piece of legislation designed to deal comprehensively with the social problems of our senior citizens. They call it the Manitoba social allowances act. A fundamental purpose of this act is to meet the financial gap in each individual case of need. Instead of a means test being applied to the particular case of need of a senior citizen, a needs test has been applied. It means, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Manitoba

is going to make sure that no senior citizen finds himself or herself in need from the standpoint of the basic necessities and services. This includes housing, food, adequate hospital and medical care. Complete medical and surgical care, including dentures, spectacles, hearing aids; all the other needs of the older members of our society are going to be met by this new provincial approach to the problem.
Before we are asked precipitously to authorize an across the board increase at this time I think the responsibilities of other areas, even down to the municipal level of government, where again there is some welfare responsibility, should be taken into consideration. Certainly this house would have all that information at its disposal.
As I understand it, the chief argument in the present debate has been that there must be an increase in payment to our senior citizens because of the continuing rise in the cost of living. It is quite true that Canada has been, as have all the economies of the west, passing through a continuing inflationary spiral, again we must keep the problem in its proper perspective and focus because the period of rapid inflation was between the years 1939 and 1951. In fact, I read a book not so long ago entitled "The Great Inflation 1939 to 1951". During that period the price index base of 100 in 1939 soared upward to somewhere in the 190's, and then it was restabilized in 1949 at an index of 100. Since that time, as some hon. members in the house have pointed out, we have reached a new index of 127 plus a few points. Since the restabilization of our price index we have not seen the rapid spiral that we had during the years of the war and immediately following. Actually since 1957, the upward movement of prices has been relatively slow indeed. Therefore, even when we look at this amendment from the standpoint of the increase in the cost of living it requires very careful thought on the part of hon. members.
In conclusion, may I say I think that in spite of the slow start to which I referred in Canada's approach to this social problem, along with all the other social problems with which we have been confronted during this century, in recent years we have shown a much greater willingness to meet the challenge of the situation from a non-partisan approach point of view. We have been willing to look at the actual social circumstances and adopt our policy to the social needs.
Unfortunately, in the early days our whole social welfare program tended to become somewhat of a jerry-built structure. We would pass a bill here to bolster up this sagging section of society, and then we would place

another bill on the statute books there to deal with another aspect, and most of those solutions were, as I have indicated, financial payments designed to encourage the people of Canada to vote for a particular political party because it gave us so and so. How many times have I heard that phrase on the hustings: Vote for us because we gave you such and such a piece of social legislation. As the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) expressed it so explicitly, governments give nothing other than that which they take from the taxpayers of Canada.
In a modern society it is the responsibility of governments not only to give financial help but to consider all the issues. With the resources for research, with the resources for investigation, with the responsibility that governments have in the modern world for providing an adequate program to meet the social needs of an urban and industrial society, it is the responsibility of the government to implement broad policies. I have confidence in the present government and believe that by the approach already taken in the Clark report, through amendments to the social security program that have already taken place and by the government's continuing negotiations with the provinces and the municipalities in respect of their important roles in carrying out a comprehensive and adequate social welfare program, we are getting for the first time a realistic approach to the problem. Let us be done with auction sale bidding.
I am glad that the amendment to the amendment presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicates that they have seen the light in this regard and have now discovered it is necessary to take a broader approach. Our senior citizens are assuming an increasingly important role in our society today. Voluntary groups and all levels of government are becoming aware of their responsibilities to the pioneers of our society. I have confidence that their growing needs will be met in adequate fashion by this administration, and certainly by being confronted with this want of confidence motion, so unexpectedly and precipitously presented to the house today, we are not going to move forward in this direction. Therefore I cannot support it.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that since opening the debate today I have been rather disappointed at some of the turns the debate has taken. Unfortunately we have seen the usual contest between the Liberals and the Tories as to who did and who did not introduce or enlarge upon social legislation. We have seen a great cloud of dust raised by the political 79951-0-411i

battle between the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). Furthermore, we have seen a subamendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) which to my mind seems to cloud the issue further. In addition to the dust covering the original intent of the amendment we now have fog mixed with the dust so that if we keep on going we will wind up in smog.
I understand that the Liberal leader in the province of Quebec has put forward the new idea that unemployment is under the jurisdiction and the responsibility of the provinces and the Leader of the Opposition apparently wants to put responsibility for old age pensions back on the provinces as well. Maybe this is the trend of the new Liberalism about which we hear so much.
We have heard complaints about short notice of the amendment, but surely this matter is not something that has suddenly been sprung on the house. If hon. members have been paying any attention whatsoever to their constituencies, surely this is a problem of which they are well aware. If they have any appreciation of conditions in the country, surely the amendment does not constitute a surprise sprung on them at the last minute. We have also heard nice words from hon. members on both sides of the house indicating their support for our old age pensioners but at the same time they do not want to do anything about the problems of these people if they can find some way of putting it off. Nice words are fine but they will not buy very much food for old age pensioners this fall or help them to have fires in their stoves unless we can run off enough reprints of the nice words we have heard today to supply our pensioners with fuel for the winter.
I hope we have not lost sight of the problem with which we are faced by reason of all the diversions I have listed. It is not the Liberal party of 1923 or the Conservative party of 1931 that is going to have to deal with the problems facing old age pensioners today. It is the members of the government and other members sitting in this house a few days before the end of the session who are going to have to decide if they are going to do anything for the old age pensioners other than utter kind words about them. We are going to have to make a decision before the end of the session so that the old age pensioners will know whether they are going to have to face another bleak winter before the government has another opportunity to do something for them.
