Mr. Speaker, the subject matter raised by the amendments before the house is of such a nature that I feel the opportunity given to speak on this subject should not be passed up. The manner in which these amendments are raised and the fact that they have been brought before the house at this late date causes one to question the seriousness of the problem in the minds of those who raised the subject, and the seriousness with which they have put forward the matter at this time.
Lately we have seen speculation in the press about when we might have another federal election. It would seem that these amendments and the words that have been spoken by members of the official opposition and the C.C.F. party indicate there is a guessing game going on amongst them as to when we might have the next federal election. Their desire to have material available when that campaign does commence has impelled them to bring this matter before us at this late date in the session, and to get words on Hansard so that they would have some material for the hustings.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, not without some basis. During my time in the house there has been an awful lot of double talk. This double talk is being carried forward today. When I say "double talk" I refer to it from the point of view of considering matters before the house, especially matters that have to do with spending programs of no small measure. There must be some road up which we are going, some consistent pattern that is being kept in mind in relation to the problems that are before the government of the day.
Much has been said about the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Conservative party during the election campaigns. I took part in the campaign of 1957, at which time I was not successful. I took part also in the campaign of 1958, when I was successful to a much greater degree than was necessary to gain me a seat in the house. In the campaign of 1957, and I think this holds true for most of the Conservative members who are here today, I would say there was a consistent presentation made to the electorate concerning the urgency of some of the problems of that day and the immediate steps the Conservative party, if returned with power sufficient to form a government, would take. Although I was not privileged to be a part of the group that formed the government in 1957 I was

glad to return to the campaign in 1958 on the basis that the promises that were made to cover the urgent problems during the election campaign of 1957 had been kept by the Prime Minister and the party of which he is the head.
In the 1958 campaign it was plainly stated to the public that those things which had been urgent and with which we said we would deal had been dealt with in the session of 1957-58, and we were now asking for a mandate from the people that would give us a tenure of office of some four years or more in which we could with authority, carry forward a long range program containing measures which were not going to be of immediate benefit but would take time. In my opinion we have consistently followed the road in that direction.
I am proud to be a member of this government. I am proud the Prime Minister is my leader. He is a national figure in Canada whose status does not require any build-up from me. His status is recognized and it is evident, from what is taking place in this house and from the speeches made by the opposition, that his stature is so great that, regardless of the guise under which they bring matters before this house, they want to try to destroy his stature. They have not made much progress to date, and I suggest they will make even less progress as the Prime Minister's stature becomes greater and greater.
The amendment put forward by the C.C.F. is a motion made by a group in this house whose aspirations to become the federal government have over a great many years made absolutely no progress, nor will they within the foreseeable future. There is practically no hope that they will ever be saddled with the responsibility of carrying on the government, initiating government policy. This fact, therefore, leaves them free to speak without restraint and to suggest further commitments on the government without any consideration of the problems that would be involved. We continually hear from them, therefore, during the days, weeks and months, suggestions which if implemented, without any exaggeration would probably add billions of dollars annually to the expenditures of this government. To them $200 million is nothing. It is nothing where they have no power and no responsibility.
But we can judge the party by their record. My friend the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) will not like this because the last thing he wants to hear anything about -and he has said so more than once-is the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan. But where the C.C.F. party have power they have

a record; and those of us who live in Saskatchewan and those of us who read and see the reports can judge them on the record.
I well remember the early days of that movement. I remember a program of socialization, land under lease and things of that sort. In the main I remember a program of social welfare, of humanity first; a program whereby they were going to institute industry and business in Saskatchewan under state control. The money that flowed in the front door and out the back door of those enterprises was going to be of such magnitude that we would have medical care, health care, hospitalization and education and we would not have to pay one cent of taxes.
That is not an exaggeration. To my hon. friend who is sitting down there at the other end of the chamber looking at me and who is now going to take off his glasses and clean them so that he can see better, I suggest that all he has to do is to go back and read the Leader-Post.
What a paper to read.

In those days it printed these things and they were never denied. Read the Regina manifesto. Read the speeches that were made by the present premier or by others of the C.C.F. party that formed that government when they came to power in 1944. Then look at the record. Those industries that were going to provide the funds are defunct. The state could not run them. They could not operate them. They could not compete in the business world. The product they made was not suitable to the public need. As to their blankets, they were obliged to give them away and use them in institutions. As to the shoes they made, the co-operative stores could not even sell them. And so the record goes with regard to the things they produced that were going to provide the money to pay for all these benefits.
Therefore if I have some reservations and doubts about socialism, it is on the basis of experience. When I say that there is double talk I mean that here is a group representing the socialist party whose record is before you in Saskatchewan, which can speak very well without responsibility; but where they have responsibility in Saskatchewan, with agriculture in the position in which it is supposed to be, when a suggestion is made that they remove the taxes on farm fuel and provide farm fuel for farmers' trucks which in effect would have meant a reduction in provincial revenues of an amount as to which we saw many figures-one of the C.C.F. campaigners said it was $200 million; the attorney general in a speech said it was $5 million-they said, "We cannot afford it; what do you want us to cut down on; where

can we get extra revenue?" But here, when they blithely talk about federal expenditures that will exceed $200 million, they can do it when they have no responsibility. However, where they have responsibility in the provincial field when a suggestion is made that might help an industry that is the foundation of the province in which they form the government to the extent of $2 million or $2,500,000 or $5 million, it is said to be beyond all possibility; they accept no responsibility; they can do nothing about it.
In Saskatchewan the municipal taxes per person on the average are the highest in Canada. That statement has been made a good many times and I have never seen it denied. That is the position of a party that, as I say, provides this double talk. While they are doing it, of course, they continue to make insinuations and to build up the idea that members of the government have no regard for the plight of the people in the old age pension group, the old age assistance group, the blind assistance group and many other persons in groups that need any sort of aid. They assert that they are the sole group that bears in mind these needs and the sole group that propounds a policy to meet those needs.
Here again there are two areas in the old age field. One is the group eligible for old age security which is universal and contributory and the other is the old age assistance group. That is the group from 65 to 69 who, on the basis of need and by a means test, can obtain a pension of, I believe, up to $55 on a shared basis between the provincial and federal governments. This is assistance that is granted in most provinces of Canada on this basis. But in Saskatchewan where we have this party of socialists or what are presumed to be socialists, with policies that are not supposed to be orthodox financially but are supposed to be different; where we have had a finance minister now retiring as of August 1 who has consistently followed a pattern of balancing his budget, so he asserts and reducing the debt and so on, who followed a very orthodox pattern but when any demands were made on the provincial government has pleaded inability to meet them because of the requirement that he follow that orthodox financial procedure; where we have this party in power, in a field where supplementary benefits are granted in many provinces of Canada, the supplementary benefits in Saskatchewan have a range presumably of $2 or $2.50 a month to a maximum of $10 and the means test they impose with regard to those supplementary benefits is of such a vicious nature that the average person receiving those supplementary allowances get in the neighbourhood of $2.50 and $3 per

Old Age Pensions
month. In other provinces where we do not have this great humanity first party-in provinces such as Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and Manitoba-I believe supplementary allowances are paid of a higher average and they are not confined to the old age assistance group but are also paid to any person qualifying for the old age pension. If that statement is in error, I stand to be corrected. However, that is the information I have.
Hence when the speakers for that party, from that small group in which they are represented in this house, rise in their places and on the basis of their claim to being this great party speak without reservation, without restraint and without responsibility at a time like this in a session of this nature, when the only purpose is not to benefit the persons to whom they wish to refer but rather to draw a big red herring for political purposes across the deliberations of this house, then I say they have left themselves open to the criticisms I have levelled at them.
I do not intend to go back and chastise the people in governments prior to this government for what they may or may not have done. However, I say this. With a desire to bring about measures that will be of lasting benefit to the groups in our country that need assistance, this government since it took office has moved steadily up the road whose path is straight, and its aims and objectives have been reiterated many times by our Prime Minister. In 1957 we raised the old age pension from $46 to $55. That was a step in the right direction. We also reduced the requirement for those who would be entitled to the pension from a domicile of 20 years to one of 10 years. That was another step on the same straight road in the right direction.
Following that we gave consideration to the position of the pensioner who for medical reasons had to leave this country for a warmer climate. This session we have brought in amendments which permit these pensioners to leave this country in the season of extreme weather conditions providing since their 21st birthday they have for a period of 25 years made their contributions to the building up of this country. And they can leave the country forever, if they so wish, and go to a warmer climate where the amenities of life are greater than they are in some areas of Canada. They can go to a foreign country if they like where they have sons or daughters or relatives with whom they can share their expenses. So that throughout the history of our tenure of office we have been moving in a steady direction.
I think the contribution of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) was one of the best I have heard to this debate. It is my experience, which backs up the remarks he made, that considering the plight of these people in terms of money only is not sufficient, that it is too narrow an outlook and does not solve their problems. I have seen a couple of old age pensioners who were well housed and had sufficient means but were very unhappy, isolated and lonesome. We have seen the development of pioneer villages, quarters where these people will have separate facilities but where they will be in association with people of like nature. We have seen a development come about whereby their needs have not been overlooked, such as a recreation hall, a community centre, where they can gather together and share their troubles, their joys and their recreations. So I say that money alone is too narrow a basis from which to look at this situation.
I think the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) in his remarks in this debate showed some doubts about the C.C.F. motion in the setting of a figure of $75. He does not know whether it is enough; he even suggested that it might be too much. That is not a very sound basis for presenting a spending motion to this house. I think the people of this country are fully aware of the demands on government today. I think they share in the universal desire that a country with the resources and the areas we have should develop in a manner and with the responsibility which will provide some measure of security for them to share in and work and sacrifice.
Along with that, I think even the person to whom these benefits flow is realistic enough to know and has known through the years when he was sacrificing and serving and working that government without responsibility, government which goes hither and thither, government which tries to cater to one segment against the over-all interests of the country is not government that can survive. So in this day I say we are moving steadily along the road which our Prime Minister has indicated is the policy of our party which he desires to follow. We may be moving along it more slowly than had been hoped, but if this is so I suggest there are good, sound reasons that the public of Canada, the recipients of these benefits, accept and realize.
Since we have come into power we have not had an easy time of it. We have had to fight a recession in peace without the benefit of war, as always happened to our friends to bail them out.
Did the hon. member say the benefit of war?

They always got bailed out of their recessions by a war. Tell me one time when they faced a critical problem involving money when war did not get them out of it? They took over power in 1935 but never got us out of the recession of the thirties. I was in business and know something about it. I was in Saskatchewan where we not only had a recession to face but we did not have a blade of green grass. I well remember that 1937 was about as bad as any year of the thirties had been, and we got out of it after war was declared in 1939. Liberal policies, Liberal programs and Liberal foresight never got them out of a recession.
Then things steamrollered and went along. We were in war and money meant nothing. Everyone realized we had to protect ourselves and carry on. During that period there was unspent purchasing power built up and after the war that carried us on. Then we were hit with a slump and had unemployment. Did Liberal policy get us out of that? Not to my knowledge. The Korean episode got us out of that. They were the 22 golden years of Liberal reign. Then there was an abundance of Liberal policies. There was an abundance also of rainfall and many other things, and countries which had been destroyed and had no industries came back into world markets to purchase.
Then we came to the position where the Liberal government was in a very critical position. The public did not know it, the Liberal government never told them, and that was the only thing which saved their bacon on this occasion, the third time in 22 years. Then the people kicked them out and we found out that they knew all the time that there was a depression on the doorstep and that they had no policy or program to get us out of it. That is the record of the Liberal government's programs and policies as far as getting us out of a depression is concerned.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

Yes, when I am through, if I have time. I think I have said enough about the double talk of the C.C.F. party, although I have not even talked about the Liberal party yet and may not have much time to.
The chief spokesman in this debate for the Liberal party was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I must say that apart from the parade which takes place on the lawns outside this house at ten o'clock every morning, the hon. member for Essex East is probably the greatest tourist attraction which we have in Ottawa. Certainly his name is

known far and wide over Canada, certainly in all the places he has visited. I have had occasion, as I mentioned before, to have him visit my area and we welcome him any time. He is a sociable, decent sort of fellow to come in, but I want to get back to his performance in this house.
How about getting back to the amendment?

I have been talking about it all the time just as consistently as other members of your party and of the Liberal party who have spoken about it.
The hon. member for Essex East in his contribution to this debate spoke in words which I think, by and large, supported the amendment proposed by the C.C.F. Certainly I thought he was very much more definite in his pronouncement that this was an urgent matter regardless of the record of the government of which he played a part and regardless of any dilly-dallying they may have done with problems of this sort which faced them.
The hon. gentleman said that it was this government's responsibility, that there could be no question about the urgency of the matter, that it must be dealt with immediately. It was either the leader of the C.C.F. group or the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) who said that as they analysed the proposal it would cost some $200 million. In supporting a measure of this nature I am just wondering what way the hon. member for Essex East is going. I cannot help but wonder from what sort of base he was operating. Was it from a base purely of political expediency or from a base of a sincere recognition of the need of these pensioners?
I have sat in this house during the past two years and on many occasions have listened to the hon. member condemn in no uncertain terms the policy of this government, the size of its budget and the size of its deficit. The hon. member has made those criticisms during the present session. On one occasion I heard the hon. gentleman suggest that the unemployment insurance should be expanded to make benefits payable to people who were off from work due to illness. Today I heard him support a measure that would add $200 million annually to the budget of the government.
I find it impossible to follow the arguments the hon. member has presented to this house. I say that he is a great actor because whether he is on his feet criticizing the government for expending too much or criticizing it for failure to spend more he seems as sincere, enthusiastic and vigorous in debate on both sides of the fence so no one knows which side really means the most to

the hon. gentleman. When the hon. gentleman is on his feet propounding the theory he has that this government's actions are restricting our trade and hampering us in expanding our world markets he seems very sincere and when he rises in his place to say that we should ban Russian automobiles and impose a tax on small cars coming in from Britain and France he seems equally sincere. I do not know what policy the hon. gentleman really espouses.
This is not a matter with which one should play politics. I am sure that every hon. member deeply and sincerely wishes to see this country develop a splendid system of security for its pioneers, for its people who are second to none in the world. I say this cannot be done by moving in several directions at once without regard to the over-all picture.
I had a thought which may not mean very much but I should like to express it. I know that in 1957 when the Liberals raised the pension from $40 to $46, Mr. Harris in bringing the proposal before the house said that in view of the position of the Canadian economy this increase was one which the economy could afford but beyond that the government could not go. I believe that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in speaking today suggested that $65 might now be a more appropriate figure. That is just more double talk. I have sat and listened time after time to hon. members opposite criticizing this government because the Canadian economy is not developing rapidly enough and the policies of the Conservative government are restricting its expansion. Yet within a matter of three years from the time when in the view of the Liberal government the economy warranted a pension of only $46 a month hon. gentlemen opposite argue that the Canadian economy warrants the payment to old age pensioners of a pension of $65 a month. It must be remembered that today there is a larger group of pensioners. Hon. gentlemen opposite by their own statements have indicated that the economy has expanded under the Conservative government if they feel that the economy can reasonably afford a payment of $65 a month. I would want to examine the situation carefully before I would claim that that is so. However, this admission is based on their own contributions to this debate.
In conclusion let me say I am proud to be a member of the government headed by the Prime Minister. The people of Canada know his sincere and deep interest in the problems that have been debated here today. The Canadian people are not unaware of the difficulties this government has experienced since taking office. The people know that this

government would not be so irresponsible as to serve one segment of Canada by moving off in the direction and to the extent suggested by the amendments proposed today. Consistently, within the means of the government and without increasing the burden on the people, this government is moving along the path leading to those things the Prime Minister set out in his platform and in his proposals to the Canadian people. As long as we hold office under his leadership we shall move steadily forward.
I shall not support the amendment. I shall continue to support a government whose path is clear, a government that is moving toward the objectives it set for itself before it took office.

gentleman was good enough to say that he would answer a question of mine. My question is the following. The hon. member did not say that.

Just to keep the record straight, Mr. Speaker, let me say that to the best of my knowledge and belief I was never on television in Toronto in my life.

Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to a weird and wonderful speech. The hon. member was supposed to be discussing the amendments before this house and he took the full period of time available to him. His speech consisted of not less than a 20 minute diatribe against the Saskatchewan government, a five minute diatribe against the Liberal party, a five minute period which he devoted to scratching the back of his leader and he spoke not one word on the amendments. The hon. gentleman

certainly received the courtesy of the house in not being called out of order.
I said it was a weird speech. The hon. gentleman began by saying he had been listening to a lot of double talk. He immediately followed that by almost weeping tears over the fact that a matter of such importance as this should have been raised by this group at this late stage in the session. I never heard such unadulterated hypocrisy as contained in that sentence, that at this late date this important issue should have been raised by the C.C.F. The only reason we have raised it is because the government has utterly failed to do so. I get my inspiration from above; where you folks get it God only knows.
Oh, oh.

May I point out to my hon. friends that we have the right to question the sincerity of the attack on us because the matter is raised at this stage of the session. If it is wrong to raise an important issue at this time because you happen to be in the opposition, then what does the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) think about the bill of rights being introduced at this stage of the session? What does he think about the important issue of national defence being referred to the committee so late in the session that the committee has not yet had an opportunity to complete its hearings and report?
What about the amendment?

What does he think about the special committee appointed to study such matters as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? I suppose it is quite all right if you are a government member and it is done by your leader; but it is completely wrong if somebody else things that perhaps while the house is sitting and responsibilities have not been accepted by the government certain matters should be raised.
You would look good in Hyde park.

Or the Conservatives of Saskatchewan.

You always had the right.

This is a most important issue. I can tell the hon. member for Regina City, even if the Conservatives want to forget it, that during the last election it was mentioned quite often. I tell the hon. member that I know of no one party, one leader or one candidate in that campaign who was not very much exercised over the predicament, the condition or the plight and the needs of the old age pensioners. I do not know one party, one leader or one candidate who was not going to do something about it is he was elected.
We did.

The Conservatives obtained a majority; they elected 208 members. Did their promises not mean anything to them?
Speaker after speaker on the Conservative side has told us that we have moved the amendment but we do not understand the difficulties, the problems and the hurdles that have to be overcome. Did you realize that when you made those campaign promises? If you did, you must have known that you were going to have to do something about them, and if you did not then you were making empty, completely empty, promises with no intention of doing anything about them.
Promises at election time are futile unless something is done about them. Considerable time has elapsed since the election of 1958. As speakers from our group have pointed out time after time, there has been an increase in the cost of living of old age pensioners. The fact is their standard of living

is going down. It must go down when costs go up and their pensions remain stationary. We are asking, as we can only ask, the government to give consideration to the advisability of fulfilling its promises and doing something now. We suggest $75 a month be paid to the old age pensioners.
We hear so much-we have heard it today -about the pioneers of Canada and of how much we owe them. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), the old age pensioners can appreciate that but they cannot pay the rent with it and they cannot eat it. They are in a difficult position, in a much more difficult position than most people who work on a job and who can fight through their trade unions to better their condition. The trade unionist can fight, and the employer can fight through his organization and through some members or through representations to parliament. He can fight for the maintenance of his position or the improvement of it, but the senior citizens of this country if they are over 70 years of age are dependent wholly and solely on what parliament does. Surely we have a responsibility to them; we have an obligation to do something for them. Many of them are in a difficult position. I know many of them who today have to spend nearly all of their pension to pay rent. We have no rent control, therefore they have no protection.
Why does the C.C.F. government not do something for them? They had a surplus of over $3,500,000?
Why does the government of Canada not do something? Why do you not talk about what is within your power instead of what is within the power of the provincial government?
We gave them an extra pension.
Yes.
We gave the Saskatchewan government $32,500,000.
You had better give them some more.
They had a surplus this year.

I have an idea that the matter will be officially handled by the government that has received a new vote of confidence from the people of that province. I say they have led the way in the past and others have followed. I have no doubt that situation is going to continue. Of course, when you follow you just take credit unto yourself for having initiated it.
We just paid for it.

You took credit for hospital insurance which was started years before. The hon. member had better get up and make his own speech. My time is nearly exhausted.
I say that we do have a responsibility and we are asking that it be accepted. We are asking that you fulfil your promises and not postpone them any longer. If this amendment is passed it will be only an interim settlement of the promises. Do not just sit on your backsides and talk in generalities, in flowery terms, scratching the back and licking the boots of your leader. That is not going to solve the problems or fulfil the promises made in order to get elected.
At least we have a leader.
If I am to judge by the reaction I received in my trip across Canada your leader is leading you down the dark path, not the golden path.
That is wishful thinking.
As a matter of fact, we had an indication of that in the last three provincial elections.
I do not think so.
You did not even run a candidate in Quebec.
If they want me to get into that I will be glad to meet them.
You are the leader tonight.
There is a difference; you have only one; we are all leaders.
Oh, oh.
There are no sheep to follow.

Hon. members seem to be in a hilarious mood tonight or else I have really got them where it hurts, and I think the latter is the correct interpretation. I was rather surprised at the statement made by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) this afternoon who said that we in this group have never raised any issues concerning the underprivileged and those in needy circumstances except today with respect to old age pensions. He made that charge against me, as a matter of fact, and I deny it.
I should like to point out that we not only speak in the house on behalf of people in need but we try to take action outside the house even when governments fail to do so. Because the hon. member for Simcoe East made this charge against me I think he should be informed that as we could not get action from the government for assistance to handicapped persons in need the New Vista society, of which I am the only lifetime

director appointed by statute of British Columbia, constructed the first apartment building in Canada architecturally designed in every manner, shape and form in order to accommodate handicapped persons in the lower income group. We proved that it could be done. I say that we not only speak in the House of Commons on these matters but that to the limit of our ability and the extent that money is available, if we can raise it, we demonstrate outside the house that we believe in the things we espouse on the floor of the House of Commons.
From my knowledge of the situation and the needs of our old age pensioners I am sure that they wholeheartedly support the amendment moved by this party, but I do want to say that I am bitterly disappointed with the subamendment moved by the official opposition. Admittedly there are suggestions here which merit considerable study and consideration but I have to oppose it, first, because it gets away from the specific immediate need, as expressed in the C.C.F. amendment, of consideration being given to raising the allowance to $75 a month and, second, because it introduces a principle which I can only interpret as meaning a return to a means test basis of granting old age pensions.
For years the people of this country and many members of parliament fought to get away from the principle of a means test involving charity to the senior citizens of our country. We maintained that the pension was a matter of right and not charity and eventually that correct principle was established. I say it would be a retrograde step of the most serious kind to give the slightest consideration to a return to the principle of a means test. The words "in co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships" can only mean a return to a vicious principle. We fought hard enough to get rid of this vicious principle without trying to re-introduce it once it has been abolished. For these reasons I have to oppose the subamendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
In whatever time is left in this debate I hope we can discuss the matter before us on the basis of the amendment and the subamendment, the principle of fulfilling the promises made by all parties, all leaders and all candidates to our senior citizens during the last election campaign and a recognition of the need at the present time. I feel certain that a government which has found and will find all the money it needs for defence purposes and has no objection to wasting hundreds of millions of dollars on Bomarcs can, if it has any interest in its own people, 79951-0-412J

Mr. Speaker, it is customary to comment on the remarks of the preceding speaker. I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and I really could not find any meat or substance in his speech on which to comment. He started off by being very critical of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More).
He was very critical of us.
He then proceeded to follow the old political axiom that when you have nothing to say you shout. He spent about 20 minutes shouting and finally took his seat after having said very little.
Let us hear some words of wisdom now.

The general tenor of the remarks on social security has been that social security should be the objective of a free society. I do not think it is necessarily the prime objective of a free society but rather that our objective should be to attempt to increase production and improve the general standards of living and to accomplish this end without spending our time in an attempt to redistribute the benefits of the taxpayers' labours.
There are two basic forms of security, emotional security and financial or material security. The amendment and the subamendment both tend to play on the emotional side of life but they go one step further and try to introduce a new form of security, political security. The amendment calls for the expenditure of at least $200 million annually to provide $75 per month to every person entitled to old age security, and this amount is to be paid regardless of financial need. I wonder how the hon. member who moved the amendment would like to approach the unions and explain that it would be necessary to make an extra deduction from their pay cheques in order to support a retired manager of the C.N.R., a bank manager or a manager of an automobile factory, persons of that type who have very little need of financial assistance in their old age.
This deduction would be in addition to an already lengthy list of deductions and the situation will not be made any easier when employees realize that often as much as one third of deductions of this nature is spent on administrative costs. I am sure that any

Old Age Pensions
one of the eight C.C.F. members would be willing to go to Montreal, address members of the Canadian Labour Congress and tell them that the amendment introduced by the C.C.F. would require the deduction of at least $300 annually from their pay cheques, only $200 of which would be paid out in actual benefits, the other $100 being used up in administrative costs.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Is the hon. member not aware that the Canadian Labour Congress passed this very same motion at their convention?

I am well aware of that, Mr. Speaker, I am aware also of the fact that the C.C.F. members very carefully avoided explaining the cost in individual terms to the members of the congress.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was speaking he emphasized the necessity for keeping social security expenditures in line with the financial situation in the country. I must admit that I thought he was doing very well and that he was in one of his rare moods when he showed some signs of political sanity and reality. However, the mood was short-lived and he reverted to his usual tactics of Alice in Wonderland. He became very generous. He was outbidding the C.C.F. in an effort to gain votes. Then he moved the subamendment, using as his excuse the idea that the Grits could not support the principle of a pension being fixed at one level. When he presented the subamendment it was easy to understand his generosity. He was actually dealing with the funds of the provinces. The subamendment emphasized the co-operation of the provinces in providing increased pensions.
Later on the subamendment referred to old age security and old age assistance. Now it is very easy to offer to increase social security measures when you are using the funds of the provincial governments. This is nothing new in the tactics of the Liberal party. We recall that they were 28 years in introducing health insurance, and then they required the provinces to pay their share of the costs. We have now a new innovation. The Grits are going to ask the provinces to move into the field of old age security. Some mention was made earlier of the fact that there is to be a dominion-provincial conference held in Ottawa.
The hon. member for Vancouver East was requesting more money for the provinces. I am sure he will find support for that amongst other members of the opposition. I am sure

we will hear a great deal about that before the end of this session. It is so easy to advocate more money for the provinces at one moment, and then in the next ask the provinces to take over the field of old age security, which is a very expensive field. It is a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul or, perhaps I should say more correctly, it is robbing Peter to pay for Paul. I am sure that the new premiers of Quebec and New Brunswick, who will have to pay for their very expensive campaign promises, would appreciate their leader-if indeed he is their leader- asking them to take over the field of old age security. We certainly know that the province of Saskatchewan, with its socialist government, has no intention of moving into that field.
Last September we had a Progressive Conservative government elected in Prince Edward Island after 22 years of Liberal rule. We were left a legacy of debt and bank overdrafts. In fact at one time between the election campaign and the swearing in of the new government the bank notified the former premier that it was not very anxious to cash any more cheques for the province. Now the Liberal subamendment would move the provincial government into a much more expensive field. I am sorry but I do not believe our province would care to accept the subamendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition.
The subamendment later calls for a national contributory scheme in co-ordination with the existing provisions for retirement. This sounds very simple. It looks to be fairly straightforward, but I would ask hon. members to look this political gift horse squarely in the mouth. This morning in the agriculture committee one of the officials of the Department of National Revenue read one of the customs regulations. When he had finished an hon. member asked him to explain what it meant when it was translated. I think we should stop and attempt to translate this simple descriptive term "in co-ordination with existing provisions for retirement".
I interpret this term to mean simply that the government would assume full control of all pension schemes already in existence. This means the Liberal party would take over all retirement schemes, whether they be for professional persons contributing to insurance schemes, for union members contributing to a scheme within a plant or a government annuity purchased by the ordinary worker. I can just see the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) standing up in this house and, with a rather beneficent smile, telling everyone that the Liberal party has now provided these things for the people

of Canada, but very carefully avoiding mention of the fact that they had taken over complete control of the schemes that previously existed.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am opposed to social security. I have seen the benefits of social security in my own riding, and especially the results of the increased benefits that this government provided. I have received a good many expressions of gratitude from my constituents for the benefits of the Diefenbaker government. However, it is still necessary to review social security, and review it in the light of present conditions. I do not feel I can support either the amendment or the subamendment until they are taken out of the political wonderland and brought into the harsh realm of fact and reality. Then I am sure not only myself but all hon. members in this house would give them support.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleasantly surprised to read the amendment put forward by the C.C.F. to raise old age pensions to $75 a month. However, I have here a brief from the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour asking that they be raised to $80 a month.
I am also surprised at the amendment suggested by the Liberals. They should have thought of it before, when they were in power, because now the people have no confidence in them. When they were in office, they came out with surplusses of over $500 million a year, yet they raised the pensions by no more than a paltry $6 a month, which was ridiculous and was to the detriment of Canada's older men and women. I think that very fact showed that the Liberal party was shirking its responsibilities, and caused it to lose the confidence of the Canadian people.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, in failing to refer at this time to the brief submitted to the Canadian cabinet on February 1, 1960 by the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. On page 12 of that brief, here is what we find:
The old age and retirement pension The C.C.C.L.'s proposal on old age and superannuation pensions involves the following:
1.	A pension of $80 per month to men and women from age 60, under a universal old age pension plan, the cost of which would be shared by the federal government and by the provinces on a basis of three fifths to two fifths;
2.	The provision of a reasonable period of residence in Canada as a prerequisite for benefits:
3.	Abolition of the means test;
Old Age Pensions
4.	Establishment of a contributory insurance for wage earners, with a reserve fund to provide for a retirement pension of $80 per month at age 60 for both men and women. Wage earners would pay 40 per cent of the premium; employers would pay the balance required to preserve the soundness of the fund: governments would be responsible for administration costs and for writing off any deficits.
5.	Protection for existing group pension plans, leaving the door open to the establishment of further plans through collective bargaining, in addition to the plans suggested above.
6.	The establishment of suitable organizations to supervise the administration of the act and to ensure that pensions are paid to those entitled to them.
Mr. Speaker, this brief submitted by national Catholic unions on February 1, 1960, was very favourably considered by the Prime Minister of Canada. I am sure that all hon. members in this house favour increased old age pensions and even family allowances, but it must be done in accordance with the budget and revenue of the Canadian government.
In conclusion, I have a suggestion to make to the government and I hope that it will meet with its approval, because I should like the Canadian government to carry it out in the near future. I am thinking of a national lottery, the profits of which would serve to increase old age pensions and family allowances. People hate taxes. The government does not manufacture money. The government collects and administers the taxpayers' money and distributes it fairly.
I think that the establishment of a national lottery by the federal government would contribute to increase the revenue of the state, would help our old people and would also make it possible to raise family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, this has been a great year for the examination of human rights in general and the relations of the human person to the state. We had earlier in the session an extremely interesting debate on capital punishment during which we discussed at great length the rights of the individual as against the state when he is convicted of a crime and the question of whether the state has unlimited powers over the individual who is convicted of a crime. Last week, we discussed the bill of rights. In a very good three-day debate hon. member after hon. member rose to discuss the rights of man as against the rights of the state and the vital importance and the necessity of protecting our fundamental freedoms, particularly in an age when the power of the state is growing day by day.

Old Age Pensions
I am very much pleased this evening to hear a debate on a third great element of government function, namely the matter of social legislation and social security. I am also glad to see so many hon. members taking part in the debate and seizing the opportunity to examine the background and philosophy of our social security. I think more than anything else the history of this century has been a history of the conflict, if you like, or the adjustment between property rights on the one hand and the right of the individual, on the other, to a share of the general wealth of society. The last century was dedicated to the establishment of political democracy. This century was primarily attuned to the development of some phase of economic democracy and a sharing generally of the great wealth that has been manufactured by mankind in the machine age.
In the last century we had the factory acts in Great Britain and the development of the first social security legislation, beginning I believe, in Germany. As the machine age developed and as man moved away from the first notions of laissez faire, that the rights of property were all important and that no entrenchment could be made upon them, there was a change to a sphere where it was recognized beyond any question that the system of capitalism and the right of free enterprise had to be tempered with legislation to keep it under control and to see to it that the profits and the emoluments of industry and of the machine were shared by society.
I may say that as social legislation developed in this country, beginning slowly in the first part of the century and of course gaining great impetus after the depression in the thirties, the Conservative party played a great and constructive role. I have before me an address made in 1957, I believe, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) called "Distinctive Conservatism" wherein the minister listed some of the contributions the Conservative party has made across the years to the development of Canada as the social nation we know today and to restricting the unlimited powers of capitalism in our free enterprise society. The minister said this:
Our party's record in the field of social security and labour legislation has been the object of the basest and most desperate misrepresentation by our political adversaries. One cabinet minister is reported as having said ... "the Liberals have introduced all the social legislation". K he made the statement it is as false as any statement can be. Look at our party's record.
It was Sir John A. Macdonald, who, in 1873, introduced the legislation that made it possible for labour to organize into unions and even to strike
[Mr. MacLellan.l
without offending the provisions of the Criminal Code, at a time when Liberals were advocating the adoption of stern measures against employees of the Globe who were then organizing and claiming the right to strike. This measure may be regarded as the beginning of effective labour legislation in Canada.
It was a Conservative government in 1894 that by legislation set apart Labour day as a national holiday.
It was a Conservative government in Ontario in 1914 that introduced workmen's compensation.
It was a Conservative government at Ottawa which in 1918 introduced workmen's compensation for government employees and employees on government railways.
It was Sir Robert Borden who appointed the first trade union member as minister of labour- the hon. Gideon Robertson then vice president of the Order of Railroad Telegraphers.
It was under the Borden government in 1918 that legal status was given to trade unions with the statutory right to organize for collective bargaining.
It was the Borden government in 1918 which first introduced federal financial assistance for the technical training of workers.
It was the Bennett government in 1931 which increased the federal contribution to old age pensions from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. The Bennett government's "New Deal" of 1935 included legislation to provide for a compulsory weekly day of rest, the eight-hour day and 48 hour week, fair trade practices, national minimum wages, and to establish the employment and social insurance commission, and the trade and industry commission. When the King government came into office in October 1935 it referred all these measures to the courts and only weakly defended them, with the result that many of them were ruled to be unconstitutional. It was by this base political treachery that the Bennett reform legislation was destroyed.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that that statement is a shocking reflection on the courts?

I must say that the attitude shown by members of the opposition this afternoon suggested that the King government of that day opposed this legislation introduced by Mr. Bennett, and I certainly believe it was weakly defended in the courts.
They did not oppose it.

I think the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said this afternoon that it was opposed by the Liberal party of the day.
To continue the speech of the Minister of Finance, he went on:
Our party supported family allowances. It was as a result of Conservative efforts that the allowance was increased in 1949 for families with more than one child. The Liberal government appropriated the following plank written into the Conservative platform at the national convention at Ottawa in 1948. "Family allowances will be placed on a uniform basis per child, regardless of the number of children in the family."

Mr. Drew's advocacy of social security and welfare legislation can be best judged by the scope of the reform legislation which he introduced in Ontario in his first session as premier in 1944. This legislation included limitation of the hours of work to 48 per week, compulsory vacations with pay, the establishment of the Ontario labour relations board, legislation to prevent discrimination on the ground of race or creed, increased workmen's compensation and the establishment of the department of planning and development.
Pensions for the disabled were first introduced by the Conservative government in Ontario. The present federal pension for the disabled is not as generous as was the Ontario provincial pension.
That statement was of course made in 1957 before the present government came into power and made available the funds which helped to increase disability pensions.
For nearly 50 years the Liberal party has been talking about health insurance but never introducing it.
Again that was a statement made in 1957.
Today the Frost government in Ontario is in the process of calling this Liberal bluff by announcing its intention to introduce hospital insurance.
I might go on to say that one of the first old age pensions acts in Canada, if not the first, was introduced by the Harrington government in Nova Scotia in 1933.
After the depression it was recognized by everyone in the democracies of the western world that social security would have to be introduced for two reasons; first of all to provide a greater share of the national wealth for all people and, second, to provide more economic stability in our nations. This was a movement all over the democratic world in the thirties in which, I am glad to say, Canada participated. Redistribution of wealth was one of the ways which could accomplish both economic stability and social security as for example in the unemployment insurance legislation.
I feel there is much yet to be done. Our civilization has to progress in many ways yet. We have great advances to make in education. We need readily available college education for all our competent young men and women and vocational training to provide new skills for people who need those skills so badly in this machine age. We have also great advances to make in medical care; to provide more social aid for the unemployable and so on. I personally believe one of the next great advances we should make in social legislation is the provision of a retirement income on a contributory basis for all Canadians.
At the moment there are a great number of people in Canada in employer and employee plans, I believe some two million. These plans leave much to be desired inasmuch as many of them are not transferable, and if a man moves from one occupation to another
Old Age Pensions
or from one industry to another he oftentimes cannot take his retirement plan with him.
We could make great progress by establishing a compulsory contributory national retirement plan. Some of the plans we have already in existence require a contribution from the employer and the employee and are very good. I believe one of the best is the civil service superannuation plan which was considerably augmented by legislation brought in this session by the Minister of Finance. Under the civil service superannuation plan, a contributory plan, male employees contribute per cent of their salary and females 5 per cent. The contributions are matched by the government and are set aside to provide a good retirement fund.
It is easy to see why pensions provided by this fund are so substantial. If a man sets aside six and one half per cent of his income as a saving toward retirement and if it is matched by a like contribution from the government this amounts to 13 per cent of a man's salary. In the case of a man earning $6,000 a year, this would come to $780 a year which obviously will provide a good pension plan. The plan not only provides a pension for a man who retires at age 60 if he wishes, or age 65, but it also provides in the case of sudden death an insurance benefit to his widow and children. In the case where a man dies leaving a widow and children the widow will receive one half of what the contributor would have been entitled to, and each child receives 20 per cent of that amount. The plan gives retirement security as well as good protection for a civil servant and his family, and I hope the day is not too far away when this nation will consider it can afford setting up such a national contributory system for all Canadians.
I would point out that this legislation, apart from providing very much needed social security, would also help stabilize the economy of the nation. One of the great challenges to government in the last 20 or 30 years has been to try to introduce into the economy of the nation such stabilizers as will prevent a boom and bust type of economy. A retirement income plan which requires every Canadian to save a certain amount of money each year to be put aside for his retirement will help take up the burden of supporting older people of the nation and will also help put away into savings, money which can be used to build up the nation.
However, while in favour of the development of a contributory national retirement system, I am aware that everything cannot

Old Age Pensions
be done at once. Mr. Mackenzie King in his nomination speech of 1919 at the Liberal convention set forth a wide program of social legislation, much of which he was able to implement in his lifetime. At the same time it took many years to implement it, and of course there is a certain part of it even not yet implemented. The social security of the nation must be paid for by that section of our nation which is employed and working. This group can only support a certain amount of social legislation at one time.
In addition to this there is the matter of priorities, as I fully realize. At a time when the rampant inflation which followed the last war has forced up the cost of Canadian goods to the point where they are not finding the same acceptance across the world as they did at one time, we have an unemployment problem born of automation and resultant from the necessity of cutting our costs of production to meet competition from other nations. Perhaps this problem requires first claim to whatever available new social security funds can be found at the present time, to train more men to do the highly skilled work of the machine age, and also to provide unemployment work projects at the present time.
I am hopeful that as soon as the government feels the nation can afford it, it will consider very carefully the establishment of a national contributory retirement scheme. I believe that the Prime Minister's (Mr. Dief-enbaker) leadership in having an examination made of the social security scheme in the United States indicates that he feels that this should be done as soon as the nation can afford to do it. All social security legislation must wait the time when it can be paid for by the working group. As money can be found I am in favour of further social security. It is required for the stabilization of the economy, and also to the end that the law of "love thy neighbour" may become more real and vital in our nation.

Mr. Speaker, the welfare state is nothing new. We have many examples in the world today. Canada has gone a long way on the road to the welfare state. The fact that we have not rushed into it is a good thing in my opinion. No one knows better than I do coming from Saskatchewan the experiments in socialism which have affected that province. I did not intend to draw that into this debate but it has already been drawn in and I thought it would be of interest to hon. members to hear from one who lives in that province and has seen some of the experiments which have worked and some which did not.

The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) gave no diatribe but presented a well thought out answer to the diatribes that emanated from the far comer of this chamber. The hon. gentleman was a businessman in Regina throughout the first depression which everybody knows certainly was not caused by any Conservative policies.
For the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) to attempt to take credit for all the social legislation in Canada is nothing short of laughable. I do not think that even Mr. Bennett can be given credit for inventing all these things. Many experiments of this nature have been conducted in various European countries and particularly in England. Such things as unemployment insurance, old age pensions, national assistance in one form and another, minimum wages, days of rest, labour legislation and other measures have all been tried by Conservative governments and in many cases were frustrated by determined efforts on the part of the opposition.
I will not bore the house with the fights in the courts. Mr. Laskin, a notable constitutional lawyer in Toronto, has written a book about that. Hon. members can amuse themselves if they want to read his vast volume. He claims that the British North America Act should never have been a frustrating statute and that if it had been interpreted in the light of the knowledge of the special conditions existing in Canada we might have had in a great deal less time many of the reforms which took years to put on the statute books.
It was the government of R. B. Bennett that gave Canada its first wheat board act which set the minimum price of grain at 87J cents a bushel. We who farmed on the prairies in those days knew that this was the first glimmer of hope ever given to western farmers with respect to the price of grain.
Is that why they all voted for Bennett in 1935?

The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is right in form tonight. The hon. gentleman also interrupted my maiden speech in this house. Although he does not like being interrupted himself I remember counting the interruptions he made in one speech of an hon. member of this house and the total was 62 interruptions. I think that is an all-time record. When the hon. gentleman writes the history he has advised me he is writing and which I am told will be greater than anything written by Herodotus or anything written since his time I am sure it will contain a number of pages devoted to the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. When this notable history

is written I shall return to the study of history and I hope it will be as good as the hon. member says it will be.
The Liberals and the C.C.F. see eye to eye only when they think it will embarrass the present government. Otherwise they make very strange bed partners indeed. This reminds me of the story of the fellow who said, "All you have to do to understand the Liberals and the C.C.F. is to note carefully what they say about each other when they are not gathered together to embarrass the government."
The amendment suggests the payment of a pension in the amount of $75 a month instead of the $55 presently paid. Of course the figure of $75 is simply a figure pulled out of a hat. Everybody knows that $75 today is not sufficient for a person to maintain a lone establishment. It is certainly not enough to pay all the bills for heat, light, water, sewers and upkeep for a private home for one person.

What is the $55
pulled out of?
Oh, dry up.

If the sum of $75 would accomplish that we would all be happy indeed. I do not think the old age pension was ever intended to be a complete living for an individual. If you were to attempt to give a complete living to an individual in this modern age in which we all expect to drive big cars and live in modern homes it would readily be seen by those of us who attempt to pay the bills for such homes and who drive such cars that we would never be able to pay enough money to keep up such an arrangement.
In my opinion the old age pension is as much assistance as we can afford to give our senior citizens out of our taxes. I do not think we will ever be able to give them as much as they are worth. My father is still alive. He is 85 years old. He worked for 40 years as a civil servant and raised a family of seven children. Most of those years were spent under a Liberal administration. Needless to say I cannot boast about the remuneration that he received under them. He now gets along on a very small pension.
This brings me to a discussion of what this government has done about pensions. We have been raising the standard of pensions all along the line. If we had a bottomless pit from which to take money we would like to raise them all a good deal more. We raised them for some branches of the civil service. We changed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police pension act not long ago. One important anomaly that existed under the act and which has now been cleared up is as
Old Age Pensions
follows. When I served in the force and up until the time I left, if you served in the mounted police and then went overseas in the army your time spent overseas in active service did not count for your pension in the mounted police; but if you left the army to serve in the mounted police and went back into the army your time spent in the mounted police was counted for the pension in the army. This sort of thing has been cleared up. If you serve in the army and then serve in the police and go back into the army,, or the other way around, you get the same kind of pension. It is now possible to read some common sense in the pension act.
The only bottleneck is the amount of money that is available for welfare measures. I have not heard any bright ideas from anybody and I am afraid I do not have any to offer either concerning how we are going to raise more money for this purpose without increasing the taxes. I know that hon. gentlemen in the far corner will immediately jump and say we should stop spending our money on defence.
I am a little tired of hearing all this peace front propaganda. I spent seven years in one war; I am not anxious to spend any of my life in another, nor am I anxious for my children to spend any time in a war. I am as much a peace front man in theory as anybody else. I do not want to see my children or my children's children in any war, but I also know this, having lived through the late 1930's, that we might have had no war if we had taken a realistic view of the world situation and spent a little bit of money between 1935 and 1940 to set up the empire air training scheme and train the young men of Canada to fly war planes instead of wandering around looking for work.
I am no peace front man; I do not like to have to fight a war ill equipped and this means physically equipped as well in your own body. I should like to see training to keep you physically fit and particularly mentally fit; that is the way I want to live. I am no peace front propagandist. I get a little bit tired of hearing the double talk, stop spending money on our defences, let us spend it on old age pensions. It is a good idea but can we do it in safety?
I,	for one, am not ready to hand over the future of our country to Mr. Khrushchev or to any of his fellow travellers. We are going to have to raise more money for these social things; we are going to have to raise old age pensions; we are going to have to give the old age pensioners more money because it costs more to buy the luxuries we are used to. We in the Conservative party certainly do not want to deny them to our parents or to our grandparents. One of these days we

Old Age Pensions
are going to be old people ourselves and we want to have a good plan to look after our own old age.
I, for one, think that we have to put in a plan under which we contribute a reasonable amount of our salary while we are young and active to pay for our own security in our own old age. I know that the old people today cannot, of course, benefit from a savings plan. A lot of them did not have any money to save in the days when people say they should have saved for their own old age. If you are raising seven children on a small civil service salary you do not have any money to pay toward a contributory plan.
I should like to see my father get a proper living wage, but we have to get it out of taxes. That is the only way I know. I think myself when this plan is brought in some thought should be given to paying more to the single person and not double perhaps to a married couple. It is the basic income which is necessary to pay your rent, to pay for your food, and so forth and possibly $100 a month for a single person and $150 per month for a married couple might be a more sensible way of doing it than $75 apiece. I certainly have no objection to giving them more; I should like to see them get more, but it has to be a workable plan and it has to be thought out well.
I think the record of this government is such that our senior citizens can look forward to this government treating them as well as any government ever did and a good deal better. Do not throw up Saskatchewan to us. Saskatchewan is right alongside Alberta but in Alberta they pay $15 more to their old people; in British Columbia they pay $20 more. I am not in the habit of handing out bouquets to Social Crediters but the socialists need not think they are the only people who believe in social security, and certainly the Liberals should be quiet on this subject until we finish one parliament.
We have not closed the door on this legislation by any means, as they well know, and to get up at the eleventh hour and holler about what we should be doing when they did not do it themselves seems to be nothing short of hyprocrisy. I do not think this is the time to bring forward this amendment. I think this plan is being considered thoroughly and I for one will be ready at any time to implement help for our citizens.
