Mr. Speaker, the matter now before the house is fraught with emotional aspects. It is easy to exploit it at the political level. It is rather

amusing to see that the Liberal party, having finally realized that it had strayed too far from the grassroots, saw fit to use the matter of pensions and social security for its own political ends unaware how ridiculous their recent practice of overbidding has been.
Politically, Pandora's box will accommodate just about anything, but never the exploitation of human misery.
When considering old age pensions, and pensions for widows, industrial retirement plans and similar social security systems, nobody would question their necessity.
Old people who, throughout their lifetime, have contributed to the economic and social progress of the country certainly are entitled to a pension upon reaching an age where their physical condition no longer enables them to be of service, except by their experience of life; and such a pension should be adequate to provide them with the minimum comfort required for a decent life.
No one would dare deny that older women, be they widows or single, are entitled to a pension and to some help from the community.
Finally, with automation and increasing technological specialization, with our modern and accelerated tempo, social security problems are looming larger and larger.
On the matter of old age pensions, Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in failing to mention at this point the great devotion and, indeed the heroism displayed by religious communities in the province of Quebec in caring for old people.
Therefore, I am glad to pay a very special tribute to achievements such as that of the Sisters of Providence, who take a particular care of older people in the very heart of Canada's metropolis, that is in the constituency of St. James, which I represent. I have seen there nuns who devote themselves unstintingly and render an incalculable service to the whole community.
But it is not sufficient to consider the necessity of those measures; we must also consider their desirability and their adequacy within the framework of this country's social needs.
We should certainly not overlook the essential needs in this field, family assistance for instance, which we call family allowances, and which are justifiable and would call, in my opinion, for an immediate adjustment, especially in the province of Quebec, where large families are still in the majority.

Mr. Speaker, I could refer to several other similar measures such as assistance to the disabled, assistance to education and other things which are all fully justified.
Present economic factors must also be considered.
In fact, some economists have claimed rightly or wrongly that increased social security might be another step towards inflation, and that the best way of helping older people would be to reduce inflation to the minimum, so as to impart more value to the pensions they do get. However, whatever the theories of economists may be, there is no doubt that any increase in pensions, however little it may be, will help those recipients. And yet, we should not increase the security of certain citizens to the extent of jeopardizing the social security of the country as a whole. Someone has to pay for such increases which necessarily affect the cost of living, either by way of increased taxation or by higher production costs.
So, we must be very careful in this field, and in this regard, I must congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who unhesitatingly provided the aged people and all citizens in need of social security with allowances more in line with today's requirements. He did not wait twenty years to do it. Later, he called for a summary of the whole situation before taking the next required step, and there is no doubt whatsoever that in due course he will take that action.
The issue is of much greater scope than the opposition seems willing to indicate. Social security in Canada, after twenty years of Liberal rule, has shown itself to be a piece of patchwork with large gaps between the patches that were added whenever political need and expediency demanded. The last patch that was added was the hospitalization insurance. Even unemployment insurance is based on a plan which was established in England in 1920 and later discarded. Health and welfare is now costing Canadians about $5 million a day, and at this time, we are spending in a month what in 1930 or thereabout we used to spend in a whole year.
The true problems to be solved are these: where do we go from here, and where shall we stop with regard to social security? Should we revise our whole scheme so as to set up a comprehensive program integrated to the needs of our day? How can we go on patching gaps with political expediency
Old Age Pensions
as the opposition now suggests for purely political ends, making use of our aged citizens, widows and orphans?
As a matter of fact, in Canada we are still far behind in the field of social security as compared to many other nations in the world. We have hospitalization insurance, and medical insurance for the needy. We have old age pensions and widows' pensions. We have limited unemployment insurance, family allowances and a pension for the disabled. On the other hand, we have no maternity benefits; no complete health insurance, nor death benefits.
From British Columbia to Newfoundland, Canadians are living in distress through no fault of their own, and many among them are not among the unemployed. Some families have no bread because the father is ill and receives no salary. The worker who suffers some injury while at work receives compensation; but who will help the farmer who breaks his arm, for instance? Would there not be a number of disabled people who might earn their living, if we had a national rehabilitation program, in Canada?
Mr. Speaker, at its annual meeting on June 2, 1958, the Canadian Welfare Council set up a social security program for Canada. At the beginning of the brief it was stated that there was:
-a great complexity of financial and social questions inherent in any social security program. Now, those difficulties, ones that are encountered in any government system, are increased by reason of issues peculiar to Canada's federal system, where the central government, the provincial governments and the municipalities must, in varying degrees, assume responsibility in the field of social security.
Furthermore, the council is aware that, because of the lack of research, Canada does not have adequate statistical data on social security and, consequently, our knowledge in this connection is incomplete. Now, adequate information and serious research are indispensable not only for the development of a good social security program but also for its sound implementation.
The council believes that the various origins of several of our social security measures, the various circumstances which have given rise to them, the various motives which are at their basis, are the cause of most of their defects, not to mention the difficulties and misunderstandings caused by the sharing of jurisdiction between the various governments concerned. We could substantially improve the social security program of Canadians if we took the proper steps to make it a more rational and better co-ordinated organization, without necessarily having to modify its main elements drastically. Besides, such is the purpose of several of the recommendations included in this brief.
Finally, the council shares with many Canadians the interest they take in social security contrib-butory systems, such as those which are now in force in the United States and in some other countries. Nevertheless-

Old Age Pensions
I am still quoting from the report.
-the addition of this new feature, that is to say contribution to our present social security program, cannot be done, in our opinion, without first carefully considering all consequences necessarily involved.
We must consider several factors; and the question is much more complex than seems to be indicated. We must take into account several factors before talking about a social security program and before changing its elements.
And, on the basis of the same brief, Mr. Speaker, I would point out some of the questions the Canadian social welfare council pointed out as fundamental principles which should be taken into account in considering any changes in the social security program now existing in Canada.
First of all, there is this difficulty resulting from the fluctuations in the purchasing power of the dollar; and any measure adopted in the field of social security, in connection with the amount of pension, is related to that fluctuation of the purchasing power of our dollar. Furthermore, any longterm measure will inevitably have that fundamental defect. There is the further fact that, in providing a social security plan for all the employed and all the unemployed, it must be remembered that the national product depends on private initiative and that, in any such social security plan, care must always be taken to retain an incentive to private initiative and to promote a national productivity. Moreover:
One of the basic objectives of a security plan must be to protect and help the family by taking adequate means to protect it against the social risks inherent in the living conditions created by modern industrial society.
Any social security program must also be aimed, above all, at maintaining the working capacity of all persons able to work; or again, it should help them recover their working ability and become self-sufficient. Furthermore, it should promote the development of the personal resources of the handicapped, and enable them to accept gainful employment.
A minimum guaranteed income should be set, and no one should be allowed to receive an income lower than the set minimum. Any social security measure involving a means test should provide social benefits to such an extent that, added to the recipient's other resources, they would ensure a minimum standard of living and of health. On the other hand, benefits based on statutory measures of general application should not, if added to the other resources of the recipient, provide the latter with an average living standard higher than the national per capita level of consumer expenditure.
According to times and places, opinions will vary as to what constitutes an acceptable standard of living. As a result, income security measures should be revised and adjusted so as to remain in harmony with current conditions.

Much greater recognition must be given than at present to the fact that poor health is a serious threat to the maintenance of an adequate income. Therefore, any measure designed to protect the individual against indirect or direct costs resulting from sickness, for instance in the form of lost pay or medical expenses, should be included in an allinclusive social security program.
It therefore follows, Mr. Speaker, that under present conditions, any social security measure is part of a whole in which all factors are interrelated.
It must be admitted that, after 20 years of Liberal administration, we have reached the point where we have to recognize that under our present social security system, legislation passed until now have weaknesses. Therefore, emergency action should be taken to correct those irregularities and weaknesses.
Appropriate procedures should be carefully looked into in order to set up social security benefits through allowances and welfare assistance, so as to provide adequately for the financial hardships resulting from old age, unemployment, disability or death of the breadwinner and the support of children.
We should consider the possibility of developing a series of measures that would better co-ordinate what we have at present.
There is no doubt that all those measures require close co-operation between governments at the federal and provincial levels, and often at the municipal level.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly support the principles involved in the amendment. However, rather than vote in favour of principles, I prefer to vote for a positive provision to raise old age pensions, for I consider it preferable to wait for the completion of that serious study which the government has undertaken, taking into account all aspects of the social security problem.
The matter is too serious, Mr. Speaker, to be used merely as a political boomerang. I therefore urge my government to step up its study and to come forward as soon as possible with definite and well balanced proposals taking into consideration Canada's entire social complex. It is only after a responsible examination of those conditions and factors that we will be in a position to discuss the amount of the increase, and I sincerely hope that the figure will be as high, if not higher, than that suggested by the opposition without any serious study or basis.
Mr. Speaker, I have confidence in my government, and I am sure that older people in the constituency of St. James will be as well treated and protected as in 1958.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to say that I am opposed to the proposed amendment in its present form. I should like to outline the reasons for my opposition to this amendment. To begin with, I am suspicious of the motives of my hon. friends in the corner. It seems to me they must have had some premonition that the study the government has been giving the Clark report might result in some concrete legislation, and they feel they would like to get their foot in the door as the propounders of a measure for improvement of social security in Canada. I think of a very recent incident. A member of this group introduced a public bill for the amendment of a certain act after having heard the minister in charge of that department give her solemn assurance on many occasions during committee hearings that such an amendment would be made. The hon. gentleman then immediately proposed the amendment which is on record so that he will be given credit as the man who thought of this and his party will be thought of as the ones who are sincerely interested in the people concerned, while this government only follows them.
The proposed amendment says this: We will give each recipient of old age pensions in Canada an increase of $20 per month. This means the expenditure of approximately $200 million of the people's money because the money that this or any other government spends is the people's money. It will be taken from the wage earner, without regard to his circumstances, because the government has no private source of money. The amendment would result in the payment of $20 per month to the man who is presently in receipt of a very comfortable pension, who may have a private income, and it will be paid with no regard for need. I believe one of the best examples of this, perhaps, is our former prime minister who is now in receipt of old age pension. I am quite sure he needs it very badly. He will get $20 per month. A person who is in dire need will only get $20 per month as well.

I shall be glad to. I will include all former members of this house who are in comfortable circumstances and who are now receiving this pension but who do not really need it. I was just coming to that point. My hon. friend is a little impatient. Of course we have in Canada, as my friend from Athabasca mentioned, the Alberta scheme of supplementary pensions. This is based on need. We have, therefore, a record of our old age pensioners who are in need. I feel that a plan could be introduced, in conjunction with the provinces, under which this government or any other federal government could make available to the provinces additional sums so that these supplementary pensions could be increased by the amount of need.
My colleague from Athabasca failed to mention that in Alberta, on the basis of need, along with the issuance of a supplementary pension, there is included free medical care, free dental care, free optical and free hospital treatment. This is contrary to the situation, as I have been given to understand it, which exists in our neighbouring province where we now have this humanitarian socialist government, and have had for some 16 years.
In so far as the old age security pension is concerned, I should like to set the record straight for the benefit of my friends in the official opposition. They make great claims about having brought in all the measures which benefit Canadians in all walks of life. They take some credit for the $6 increase in the old age pension in 1957. I should like to remind these hon. gentlemen that this was a promise made immediately prior to the election which was to become effective on July 1 of that year. Between the time when this promise was made and the date on which it was to become effective the people of Canada had made up their minds that they had waited too long and it was therefore left to this government to provide the funds to carry out the promises made by those gentlemen who sat waiting for 22 years.

Old Age Pensions
I should like to say further that on top of the 15 per cent increase which this government gave after its predecessors had promised it in 1957, a further 19.5 per cent increase was made to bring the pension to its present level of $55 per month. The present amendment, of course, proposes a 36.3 per cent increase which is to be given regardless of need. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it can be said in all honesty that this government has shown its interest in the welfare of Canadians in all walks of life. As a member of the party which forms the government today, I am not ashamed of what this government has done.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) made a great outcry about the promises which were made on the hustings by those members who now sit on the back benches in support of the government. I should like to tell this hon. member that I did not campaign in either of the elections on promises. I campaigned on the fact that we have a Canadian leading our party whose interest in Canadians and in the country is genuine and sincere. It was my pride to win in the 1958 election on the basis of what had been accomplished in the few short months from June 10, 1957.
May I ask my hon. friend, for whom I have very great respect, a question?

I understand that earlier today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said that it was unfortunate that I, as minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare, could not be in the house to hear the discussion. I must apologize for being absent on business. I can only repeat that it is unfortunate that the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) are not in the house this evening.
As the house well knows, this is simply a supply motion. In my estimation it is too bad that it should have developed into a want of confidence motion. All social security measures are of concern to all of us. They are not the special prerogative of any one party

in the house or of any one individual member. They are the concern of all of us. But let us not forget that there is no one to whom they are of more concern than the individual who may find himself in straitened circumstances or possibly getting up in years and not being in possession of all the wherewithal with which to get by in this world.
I cannot say how much I regret-and I must use this word

the irresponsibility shown by both opposition parties in bringing forward both these amendments as they have done. I understand it has been indicated that the Liberals are going to vote against the C.C.F. main amendment and that the C.C.F. are going to vote against the Liberals subamendment. To me that indicates that they are simply vying with each other in playing upon the sympathies of those elderly people who through no fault of their own find themselves in difficult circumstances. I should like to read the Liberal subamendment, Mr. Speaker. It reads as follows:
In the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide in co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships endured by the recipients of old age security and old age assistance; to extend old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age; for the vesting of benefits in industrial pensions plans; and for a national contributory pension scheme, co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security based on federal government contributions, as well as on contributions of employees, employers and self-employed.
This indicates to me, from the way in which it starts off, that it is simply a desire to load the provinces with further responsibility. I feel that it also indicates a certain amount of ignorance of the present situation. It says "to extend old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age". This can be done at the present time under unemployment assistance. There is a phrase "for the vesting of benefits in industrial pensions plans". I should just like to reiterate what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said on May 24, 1960, as reported at page 4207 of Hansard:
The fact is that parliament has no jurisdiction to provide for vesting of pension rights.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the minister would be out of order in quoting from other debates in this session.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

May I put it in this way, Mr. Speaker? I think the Minister of Finance at that time indicated the legal position of the government so far as the vesting of rights is concerned.
I would suggest that the latter part of the subamendment is an effort to try to embarrass the government in those matters concerning the Clark report. I am going to have

quite a bit to say about the Clark report later, and I will deal with it at that time.
I feel that the record speaks for itself as to what this government has done within the short space of two years and nine months. In the field of old age security it has increased the benefits from $46 to $55 a month. It has reduced the residence requirement from 20 years to 10 years. It has increased the periods of temporary absence allowed for beneficiaries leaving the country for visits; and an amendment received royal assent, I believe it was on July 7, to make provision for pensions to be paid outside of the country. These legislative changes in my opinion afford much more generous treatment and protection than the pensioners had under the previous administration and along with the consideration being given to the Clark report clearly indicate our desire to be as helpful as possible to our senior citizens in the matter of old age pensions.
These accomplishments, as I stated in my last paragraph, have been accomplished in the two years and nine months since the October session started in the fall of 1957. We have also provided for increases in old age assistance and assistance to the blind and disabled. We removed the 45 per cent threshold on unemployment assistance which was ridiculous at that time and is now applicable in every province in Canada. We made it possible for hospital insurance to come into effect earlier than it would have come into effect otherwise. We have doubled or approximately doubled hospital construction grants.
I should just like to outline briefly the situation in connection with hospital construction grants. In May, 1948 these grants were instituted by the previous administration in the health grants schedule. In that schedule of health grants hospital construction was included, as I say. In 1953 there was a 50 per cent reduction in the hospital construction grants. I am going to admit that three other new grants were added at that time, namely the laboratory and radiological services grant, the medical rehabilitation grant and the child and maternity health grant. But nevertheless, the hospital construction grant was cut in half.
On January 1, 1958 this government, in order to assist in accelerating the hospital program, doubled from $6.7 million the construction grant and added to that doubling an amount of $4 million for major renovations of and alterations to obsolete hospitals. This was a recommended sphere of activity. I am sure that the hospitals and municipalities across the country have realized what a great assistance this additional grant has

been. As I say, it was doubled from $6.7 million with an additional $4 million added for renovations and major alterations.
I might point out that the straight active bed or equivalent assistance was increased from $1,000 to $2,000. Chronic, mental and tubercular beds were increased from $1,500 to $2,000; nurses' beds from $500 to $750. Internes' beds were instituted as a new step and these were included at $750 per bed and of course the renovations were included.
I should now like to place a few figures on Hansard as I think they are extremely interesting. I will give the total of what they call income maintenance grants. The total grants for 1956-57 in the public accounts were $814,960,572. In the year 1957-58 it will be remembered that the previous administration had made effective as of July 1, 1957 a $6 increase in the old age security. Effective as of November 1, 1957, the present administration added an additional $9 per month by which it arrived at the present $55 per month figure. The total in 1957-58, sharing an increase by both the previous administration and for part of the year by the present administration, was $959,717,252.
I should like the house to be aware of the figure which is in the estimates book for the year 1960-61, namely $1,188,300,000. This is an increase over 1956-57, the last year before any increase by the former administration or the present one, of $373,339,428, and this does not include hospital insurance. In the present estimate this total is $167 million. This, by the way, is for hospital insurance which had been promised by the previous administration back in 1919 and finally brought in in the spring of 1957; and as I said earlier we made it possible to advance the date of hospital insurance benefits becoming available to Canadian citizens.
There have been proposals to raise the old age security rate. I would suggest that any proposal to raise the amount of the flat rate pension at this time would be premature and should wait until the relation of this pension to a graduated pension benefit can be taken into consideration. I would point out that under the existing legislation the federal government will spend this fiscal year $590 million on old age security and $31 million on old age assistance.
The proposal to increase the pension to $75 a month would cost at least $226 million additional for old age security and old age assistance making a total of $847 million. It would mean contributing to the old age security fund an increase by about one third the present taxes; that is, raising the earmarked taxes on personal income, corporate income and the sales tax to 4 per cent

Old Age Pensions
each as well as further grants from general revenue for the increased outlays on old age assistance. Surely it would be unwise to make such a move prior to a careful consideration being given to the role of the flat rate benefit in relation to a graded benefit. This is particularly so with a proposal involving such very large expenditures.
I think it is accepted that Canadians generally were pleased and satisfied with the figures for which this government increased the monthly old age security, making it effective November 1, 1958, namely $55. I would like to draw attention to appendix C on page 87 of the estimates committee report No. 3, in which there is a table setting out the consumer price index in 1949 equalling 100, the old age security payment in current value dollars and in constant dollars. In November, 1957 the consumer price index was 123.3; current value dollars, 55; constant dollars, 55. We come to February 1960 and the consumer price index had risen to 127.2; the current value dollars, 55; the constant dollars, taking into consideration the increase in the consumer price index from 123.3 to 127.2, had fallen from 55 to 53.31.
I cannot feel that this is the most serious drop in the world. I have every sympathy for anybody in these circumstances and the government has all these things under consideration. But I cannot feel that a drop from November, 1957, when this government raised the pension to $55, to a value of 53.31 in February, 1960 is the most serious drop in the world.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention that I feel the hon. member for Essex East in speaking on this subamendment today must feel he is on rather slippery ground. I should like to point out what my illustrious predecessor said back in 1956 in the estimates committee, as reported on page 268 of the report. He is reported as saying:

... If there is a need-and I have acknowledged that there is need in many cases *-we on the federal side have discharged our responsibility in a respectable way. If need still exists, then in the light of the assumption by the federal government of this tremendous proportion of the total burden, I say that it is not unfair to suggest that all of the criticism should not be levelled at the federal government. I am not suggesting that moneys paid by way of old age pensions and social security are adequate to take care of the full living expenses of an individual; but I think it would be generally agreed that there is no similar social security benefit anywhere that is intended to provide for full maintenance. These are grants toward assistance, grants toward maintenance, and I believe that if there is any need of providing relief in this particular at this time, I have properly suggested the quarters whence that relief might be provided.

Apparently he meant either the provinces or the municipalities, and this of course is borne out by the terms of the subamendment. Further he says:
Already there is a great deal of criticism and a suggestion that this is extravagant, that this is the welfare state, and things of that kind that I call sinister arguments. We cannot, obviously, do these things if we concentrate all our payments in one department of activity.
I think things have changed since then because it is obvious from the subamendment before us today that there is certainly a lack of serious approach to this subject if they at that time claimed to have a serious approach. These are very irresponsible and extravagant statements contained in the amendment.
I should like to point out some of the comparisons as far as supplementary allowances are concerned, and I think it would do well for the members of the group of this house who moved the original amendment to pay attention to these figures. In old age security -incidentally, there are no supplementary allowances in old age assistance in the province of Saskatchewan-there is a supplement of $2.50 to $10 per person on an income test.
In Ontario the old age security and old age allowances are dealt with in the same fashion. The municipalities provide for the individual concerned as they see fit and the province assists up to 80 per cent of the first $20 of that supplemental allowance. There is quite a difference between $20 and $2.50 to $10. In British Columbia the old age security and old age allowances are again dealt with in a similar fashion. There is a maximum of $24 per person on a means test. In Alberta the old age security and old age assistance are dealt with in the same fashion up to $15 per month on a means test. In Manitoba there is a scheme similar to that in Ontario where the municipality decides the amount to give to the individual and the province pays 80 per cent of whatever that happens to be.
Unfortunately I was unable to be present earlier in the day and I am not sure what transpired but I understand that the hon. member for Essex East indicated that I had contemptuously-I believe his word was "contemptuously" or some similar phraseology- refused to give replies to questions on the Clark report. This is nonsense. Questions concerning the Clark report have been dealt with at great length. I feel that I should repeat some of the statements I made about the Clark report in the estimates committee. I believe that they will be of benefit to those hon. members of this house who were not fortunate enough to be members of the estimates committee during its study of the estimates of the Department of National

-to conduct an inquiry into facts relating to old age security systems in effect in Canada and the United States, with particular reference to those features of the old age and survivors insurance program in the United States which make it possible for higher benefits to be paid covering a wider range of contingencies at an earlier age than is provided under present (Canadian) legislation.

Mr. Speaker, we all know this old story. We have heard it many times. The Clark report consists of two volumes totalling 861 pages. I have both volumes here. I would venture to say that no hon. member of the opposition has read the full two volumes. I feel that this is an historic document which will be most valuable for all time to come concerning studies of this type which we are presently conducting in the department. I have no apologies to make for the thoroughness and completeness of this report.
I think it is significant that after a most exhaustive analysis of the United States and Canadian programs Dr. Clark comes to the conclusion, as stated in paragraph 905 of his report, that the 1950 recommendations of the joint parliamentary committee which led to the passage of the present Old Age Security Act were fundamentally sound. The problem, therefore, is one of deciding how best to build on what we now have. Nothing that Dr. Clark says would indicate that our present program is not reasonably good foundation for considering what improvements should be made in the future.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) expressed this same point of view in announcing initiation of the study when he said, as reported at page 3233 of Hansard of January 13, 1958:
With these facts before us we have decided that further detailed investigation and inquiry should be made-to produce the information which will enable us to determine whether a similar system-
That is, the United States O.A.S.I. I continue:

or some modification of it could be fitted or adapted to Canadian requirements-
Old Age Pensions
I should like to stress the next words used by the Prime Minister on that occasion:
-in addition, of course-and I should like to emphasize this point-to our present system. I should like to make it clear that we have no thought of weakening in any way our present provisions.
A particularly valuable aspect of the report is the light it throws on the Canadian program as compared with that in operation in the United States. Dr. Clark indicates quite clearly that in certain respects the United States system is superior to the Canadian. He analyses the two schemes at great length showing why the United States system is able to provide more generous benefits and singling out the specific areas in which it is more advantageous. He also pinpoints areas in which the balance between the two is more open to argument.
Most important of all, in paragraphs 1352 and 2041 of his report he draws attention to a finding by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects to the effect that the Canadian level of per capita income is some 30 per cent below that of the United States. Dr. Clark draws from this important statement a very clear conclusion with regard to comparative pension levels in the two countries.
The United States old age, disability and survivors insurance program, as Dr. Clark points out, is currently based on 3 per cent contributions from both employers and employees amounting to a total of 6 per cent of payroll. This is intended to rise by 1969 to 9 per cent of payroll. If we accept the fact that the average per capita income of Canadians-including those in their active working years-is 30 per cent below that in the United States, the question that presents itself is this. How can we expect, other than by establishing contribution rates that are proportionately higher, to achieve a level of pension benefits to the United States level?
It would seem, on the face of it, that if our per capita income is 30 per cent lower than that of the United States, then the same contribution rate levied in Canada would inevitably produce a level of benefits that is correspondingly lower than in the United States. If this is so, then one of the questions we should ask ourselves in Canada is whether or not we are prepared to pay contribution rates which are proportionately higher than those levied in the United States on incomes which are 30 per cent lower in order to achieve parity with the United States system.
Another point the Clark report brings out is that the United States system is based on graduated benefit levels while the Canadian employs a flat rate benefit. Although in the upper income levels, the United States system
But in Canada it is only on the net profit after taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That is right. I think we must recognize, therefore, that the imposition of a payroll tax for financing a contributory pension system would constitute a direct addition to production costs and might well have important consequences, particularly for marginal industries. It would also impose a relatively greater burden on those industries where labour constitutes a large portion of production costs as contrasted with other types of industry where automation or the nature of the operation itself requires a relatively small labour component. For example, retail stores and construction companies where labour costs are high would be affected much more by payroll taxes than pulp and paper companies or distilleries where labour costs constitute a much smaller item in the production budget.
Finally, Dr. Clark goes into the very important question of private industrial pension plans which have become an increasingly important element in the picture. Perhaps it is fair to state that when the Canadian scheme was adopted in 1950 it was hoped that industrial employers would build, on top of the flat benefit, supplemental pension provisions for their employees, or that individuals would make their own provisions through government annuities and so on. Thus by building this additional arrangement on the floor provided by the government scheme it would be possible to build a second deck which would give individuals a retirement income bearing a relationship to their previous earnings.
To some extent this development has taken place. Dr. Clark points out that there has been an impressive growth in private pension plans covering increasingly large numbers of wage and salary workers in Canada. A pertinent question is, what would happen to these existing provisions if the government should move into the picture with some supplementary program? Do we end up with a triple deck system for those urban and industrial workers, particularly in highly organized sections of the labour force, who have already been able to work out with their employers pensions supplemental to the basic government pension? Do we allow contracting out which will be permitted under the new British scheme though not under O.A.S.I. in the United States? Or do we scrap these private plans and replace them by a public supplemental scheme? If we do the latter, are we really any farther ahead? If we do not, how do we relate a graduated

Old Age Pensions
system under a new government scheme to the graduated system which private plans have already provided to some extent?
One of the outstanding weaknesses of present industrial pension plans is, of course, that they do not provide transferability of pension rights from one employer to another. This raises the whole question of portable pensions, a subject in which I am happy to note that the government of Ontario has recently taken a very active interest. Indeed, a special committee has been appointed to look into the matter and this seems to me at least to be a most worth-while undertaking.
These, then, are some of the important issues raised by the Clark report which various federal departments and agencies have been examining in the past 18 months. All have to be thought through and resolved before any final decisions can be made. The Clark report has provided a very useful background on the approach followed in the United States in relation to the possibility of modifications in the program and, along with material on the programs in other countries such as the United Kingdom and Sweden, is being studied by a departmental committee.
It is surely obvious, Mr. Speaker, that we must not make decisions on any hasty, ill-considered basis because the cost implications are very great. In all frankness, I am not in a position to say at the present time that we have reached solutions to all of these questions. But the people of Canada can rest assured that this extremely vital problem is being given the urgent consideration and study which it so clearly merits.
I think I have dealt with the Clark report at some length. I have pointed out the increase over the term that this government has been in office in social benefits of all kinds, unemployment assistance, old age security, old age assistance, disability allowances, blind allowances, the bringing into early fruition of the hospital insurance scheme and hospital construction grants, and I repeat: Let the record speak for itself. I claim that no government has ever done more in the welfare field in Canada than we have in the two years and nine months since October of 1957. We are not satisfied now. We are giving continuous study to all of these problems. Despite the great steps we have taken, we will endeavour to continue to improve the lot of those unfortunate and aged people in need of assistance.

But what an improvement.

My hon. friend says, "What an improvement." Let us examine the extent to which that statement is warranted by the facts. Old age security was introduced in this house in 1951 following a report made by an all-party committee, as a result of which the government of the day recommended to this house a program to provide for a universal system of old age security which eliminated the means test. This was the first act of its kind enacted by any government in the world.
However, this act had been preceded by the introduction in 1925 of the first old age pensions act, an act that did not become law because it was vetoed in the other place by a chamber which, at that time, was in its majority composed of members who supported the Conservative party.
Who changed that?

The people of Canada changed that when in the following election they returned the government of Mackenzie King. One of the reasons for the return of that government was a protest against the action taken by the Conservative majority in the other place.
From 1926 onward there were various refinements made in the old age pensions act. In 1947 the old age pension stood at $20, and it was successively increased from $20 to $30; from $30 to $40; and from $40 to $46. During that time the income ceilings were extended. During that time the Old Age Assistance Act was amended in proportion to the increases in the basic grant and in the income ceilings provided for in the original old age pensions act.
In addition to that blindness allowances were provided, and provided by the same Liberal government that brought forward the original old age pensions act which later became the old age security universal system that now extends benefits to somewhat between 900,000 and 1,000,000 people in this

Family allowances were introduced in 1945. Mr. Lesage took over, he immediately took a broom and began a general sweeping up, chucking everybody out, including the commission. That is perhaps the reason why he did not hesitate to accept the hospitalization insurance plan, and we shall see the results, and whether the people will be satisfied.
The hon. member for Essex East made a magnificent political speech. Obviously he will get the headlines he was after. But I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that there were, in his statement, a few inaccuracies which I ask leave to point out.
He, first of all, lengthily related the background of social security legislation in Canada. He also spoke at length on the increases of $20, $30 and $40 which were granted with regard to the old age pension plan. However, he did not specify that this increase of $20 was in respect of a period of 22 years. He also forgot to mention that, within two years, this government had raised the old age pensions by $9.
In proportion, we should say that it takes a Liberal government three times longer to pass valuable and beneficial legislation than it does a Conservative government.
He also dealt with the hospitalization insurance scheme. However, he forgot to tell us that, in 1919-and I do not pretend to remember Mr. King's statement very well -however, history tells us that, as far back as 1919, Mr. Mackenzie King had promised a hospitalization insurance scheme. And this time the Liberal party waited 37 years before enforcing the plan Mr. Mackenzie King had promised a year before I was born.
It took the Liberal party 37 years to-

I need only a few minutes more, perhaps five minutes.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it took 37 years for the Liberal party to introduce a plan conceived, devised and promised by the hon.

Mackenzie King. And today we are told that he is the champion of all social security measures in Canada.
I suggest that, before we readily agree to the amendment, introduced by the C.C.F. party which proposes to raise the old age pension to $75, there are a lot of factors to be considered.
First we should ask ourselves on what basis the C.C.F. suggests the $75 figure. Why not $70 or $80? The first thought that comes to mind, of course, is that those people have read the representations which I understand were made by the C.C.L. in favour of such a measure, and thought that perhaps in view of the uncertain possibility that a political party might eventually be born in Canada, it might be advisable to make a bit of political hay now by introducing this motion to raise the old age security pension to $75 a month.
Mr. Speaker, the figure is rather arbitrary, but I think we might consider the proposal if there were a proper balance between the old age pension and family allowances.
I am one of those who believe that the government should take care of old people, because after all, they are the ones who shaped this country as it exists today. It is because of the work of those pioneers that we enjoy our present freedom and benefits. Therefore, I am one of those who believe that nothing will ever be too good for our senior citizens.
On the other hand, if we want to protect old people, it seems to me that at the same time, we should consider the problem of our families. On the basis of a quick calculation, it is said that in paying an old age pension of $55 a month, the federal government is providing a capital of $13,200 for the beneficiaries of such pensions. Now the C.C.F. suggestion that the pension be raised to $75 a month would mean that the federal government would be setting aside a capital of $18,000 in favour of our old people.
But what is being done for the young people? If we must protect our old people, and look after them, we must also look after our growing children and consider those who face a situation which is much more serious and difficult than the situation faced by people who have already reached a certain age. Yet a capital of only $1,440 a year is set aside for our young people.
If Canada's economic and financial position is such as to warrant that substantial

increase in the old age security pension, I think we should at the same time consider raising the rate of family allowances.
Mr. Speaker, in making this comparison, I hope my words will not be construed as a plea in favour of family allowances as against an increase in old age pensions. On the contrary, I repeat that, if our financial resources allow it, let us raise the old age pension sky high, but let us at the same time look after the problem of children; let us help the children by raising family allowances to a level more consistent with the present cost of living.
Mr. Speaker the amendment to the amendment put forward by the Liberals is of special significance in that it comes at the end of an election campaign. You will recall that in the last election campaign we were promised that additional benefits would be given our older people and our children. In other words, the one upon whom the hon. member for Essex East showered stirring and fulsome praise a moment ago, has suddenly turned into a Santa Claus. He made promises that he must now carry out and he knows he is unable to do so. What has he done? He came here to meet his friends in Ottawa, he asked them to introduce some measure which would commit the federal government to fulfil the promises they had made during the election campaign.
That's childish.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville says this is childish. I agree with him that, if he clearly understood what I said, it is because my reasoning is clear.

This century, Mr. Speaker, can certainly be described as the century of social security. First of all, we were told that the great leaders (whose names were mentioned on this great day when an historic monument was unveiled) were the champions of social security measures I submit that they were compelled to follow the example of other countries. But they made a great fuss about family allowances in particular, because, in my opinion, that is what affected the population most. Besides, I would remind you that the first member who spoke about social security measures is not the one who was

referred to a moment ago, but the former member for the constituency of Saguenay (Mr. Frederic Dorion) a distinguished brother of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Noel Dorion.)
No, it was Mr. Blanchette.

And it was precisely to give in to the pressures exerted on the Liberal government at that time-who seemed to think for a moment that its ivory tower might collapse as it actually did in 1957-that the Liberal party agreed to pay certain gratuities in the form of family allowances.
Every time those people went into an election campaign, we had the impression that the level of social security measures would be raised and, in fact, it happened occasionally. They had made it a pet theme, and even in 1957, they promised that if the Liberal government were re-elected, some slight increase in family allowances would be granted and that the old age pension would be increased to $46. Well, at that time, the Conservative party without formally promising that, realized the necessity of giving increased consideration to our older citizens and the present Prime Minister then promised that if, he were elected he would raise their pensions. That is what happened, and in the space of two years, the Conservative party gave the older people of Canada much more than the Liberal party gave them in 20 years.
